subtopic: STATEMENT BY PRIME MINISTER ON PROPOSED CHARTER

speakeroldname: Right Hon. P. E. Trudeau (Prime Minister):
subtopic: STATEMENT BY PRIME MINISTER ON PROPOSED CHARTER
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it was agreed at the constitutional conference held in Victoria last week that the governments there represented would advise the secretary of the constitutional conference by Monday, June 28, whether they accepted the Canadian constitutional charter, 1971. I wish to advise the House that the government of Canada has today advised the secretary that the charter is acceptable to it.
While the government is prepared to accept the charter and to recommend its approval to the two Houses of Parliament, I want to make it clear that the federal government regards it as a compromise. The provisions of the charter do not, in several respects, represent what the government would have preferred. This is the nature of all negotiated agreements where there are substantial differences of opinion to be accommodated. The essence of agreement is concession and the federal government, before and at Victoria, made concessions on a number of matters which it regarded as important in order that agreement might result. This was equally true, I think, in the case of the provincial governments. I think one could say that the charter is a good compromise in the sense that, even though no government got exactly what it wanted, every participant felt that Canada and Canadians generally would be better served with such a document than without it. That being the nature of compromise, and therefore the nature of the charter, it is a matter of particular disappointment and regret that the government of Quebec has decided that it is not prepared to accept the charter as it stands.

There is perhaps some slight ground for encouragement in the fact that the statement by the Prime Minister of Quebec suggests that the reason for the rejection by the Province relates to one part of the Charter only- what he referred to as "uncertainty" in relation to the meaning and effect of Articles 44 and 45 of the Charter which constitute the revised version of section 94A of the British North America Act. I made it clear, in reply to questions by the press in Toronto on Wednesday, that if the Government of Quebec has specific suggestions to remedy whatever uncertainty concerns them, the Federal Government will receive them with an open mind and will, if necessary, communicate with the Premiers of the provinces to see whether there might be any means of meeting this problem that would be acceptable to all concerned.
I must, of course, at the same time emphasize that one cannot consider that the Charter is indefinitely open for acceptance. Parties to a compromise cannot be considered to be bound by it, or to any part of it, unless the agreement that it was intended to achieve emerges within a reasonable time.

It will of course be a matter of disappointment if the charter does not eventually complete the course that was contemplated for it-with debate and approval by legislatures and both Houses of Parliament. I am convinced that it would constitute a major advance for Canada. I think too that it would provide a means gradually and progressively to adapt our total constitution and build a better future for all provinces and for the country as a whole. But if the charter is not accepted, our country will still go on. As I said at the opening of the constitutional conference at Victoria, constitutional revision is a formidable undertaking: a challenge of great dimension for all Canadians. It will be achieved only through mutual understanding, patience and compromise. But whether it is achieved early or late, one day it will be completed. In the interim-and after its achievement-our task in government and in Parliament is to make real the great promise of our future within a united Canada.

Mr. Speaker, I trust the House will forgive me, in my almost impromptu response to the Prime Minister, if my remarks are not as polished and finished in form as they usually are. Nevertheless, I should like to make two or three comments on the Prime Minister's statement.
I am encouraged by the suggestion in the statement that discussions on constitutional reform can and will continue whether or not what has been named the Victoria charter is adopted. I make no comment this morning

as to the contents of the charter or as to how satisfactory they are. The Prime Minister himself has expressed some disappointment, and it may be exaggeration to some extent to describe this package as a charter. However, what I really wish to call to the attention of the House this morning are one or two ambiguities in our present situation.
First, is the Prime Minister of Canada in his statement extending the June 28 deadline, or is he indicating that as far as his government is concerned it is prepared to extend the deadline? This is not clear, I suggest, in what the Prime Minister has said this morning.
Second, in commenting outside the House the Prime Minister made remarks which suggested that in his opinion constitutional reform was not very important. I might say that in view of that I was rather surprised to find him making a statement on the subject this morning. I ask him, however, to consider very earnestly the effect of the impression he gave outside the House that constitutional reform is, after all, not very important and that we can continue to get along without it. I ask him to consider what effect this impression will have upon the importance the people of Canada as a whole attach to continued discussions, the effect it will have upon the importance that the provinces generally attach to continued discussions and, indeed, the willingness of provinces that do not attach too much importance to constitutional reform to continue to be involved in the laborious process of constitutional discussions. If the Prime Minister believes continued discussions and the achievement of reform are important he should without hesitation make this abundantly clear to the people of this country.
I say without hesitation that I believe constitutional progress is important in Canada. I was not at Victoria but from what I have heard I have the impression progress was made in the discussions there. I think it would be a pity if this were lost. I repeat that I believe it is important that these discussions continue. I believe it is important that the Prime Minister make this clear.
I recognize there are other urgent matters for us to consider in Parliament and to which the government of Canada and other governments should devote attention. I believe we can do both. I do not believe we should defer these other important matters for constitutional discussions. But I say in all earnestness that in my opinion, while I understand fully the impatience felt in many parts of the country about the time being spent on constitutional discussion and while I understand fully the regret with regard the decision of the government of Quebec, for the future of this country it is important that we recognize the importance of continuing these efforts and it is important that we press forward and discharge our responsibilities.

Mr. Speaker, it is of course regrettable that agreement could not be reached at Victoria. I want to emphasize the precise words I have used because I think the people of Canada may have received an incorrect impression. There was not agreement reached at Victoria. That is why it was necessary to
have some time for the respective cabinets to consider whether or not they would agree to the document prepared in Victoria. The real regret is not that the Prime Minister of one of the provinces of Canada has said no to the charter. The real regret is that at Victoria no agreement was in fact reached among the 11 heads of government. No agreement was reached by the 11 heads of government for reasons that I, of course, do not know even though I was in Victoria, because I was not able to attend the closed sessions.
I say, Mr. Speaker, I do not entirely blame Mr. Bou-rassa for hesitating to agree to the so-called charter because I suggested to some friends of mine in Victoria that the revised 94A was pretty confusing in that the language left entirely in doubt which level of government would in fact have priority in the legislative fields indicated even in the suggested amendment to 94A. I read a few days ago in a western paper-I do not have the clipping with me but I think my memory is correct- that in an interview the Prime Minister in reply to a question by Claude Ryan, said that he was not quite sure how the court would decide if there were a federal law dealing with family allowances and a legislated Quebec plan of family allowances and the two conflicted. He was not sure exactly what would happen if a court had to decide the issue. I think the Prime Minister said that. He nods assent to my statement. If that is the case, then it must be obvious to any thoughtful Canadian that it would not have been very easy for Mr. Bourassa to accept the charter if the Quebec government was seeking, as it was, priority in the fields that were added. I am not saying whether it should have it, although personally I have great sympathy with their desire in that direction. But if that is what it was seeking and it was abviously not getting it, it would have been far too silly to expect the government of Quebec to say yes to the charter, having no absolute certainty as to precisely what it had in the amended 94A and the possibility that in fact it had nothing at all.
The Prime Minister said in his statement-and of course one agrees with him-that in any such difficult job as rewriting a constitution, compromise and give and take are necessary. I suggest respectfully that that does not mean deliberately confusing, uncertain and ambiguous language, because if there is one thing that our constitution should try to avoid, or it will never succeed, it is deliberately ambiguous language.
The Prime Minister has said, not in the House but outside, that Mr. Bourassa was faced by a very small opposition. He paid the compliment to the few hundred members of my party in Quebec that they were heading the opposition. I wish they were strong enough to do that. I appreciate the compliment. But the fact is-and it must be obvious to all Members of Parliament and to all the people of Canada if we are to write a new constitution and retain a united country, as I and all members of the House want to do-that the opposition to this so-called charter appears to be unanimous apart from some of the

Mr. Speaker, I suggest (a) that the constitutional discussions must be continued, and (b) that the situation in Quebec and the attitude toward the charter by all political parties in Quebec at least, if not of the majority of the people as I think is the case, must be taken into account in drafting constitutional changes. There must be understanding of both of those objectives, and accommodation made to them, if Canada is to remain a united country.
I want to conclude by saying that I agree with the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Stanfield) that the word charter, applied to the document arrived at in Victoria, may be an exaggeration. But in any case I hope the discussions will continue and that they will from now on be based on economic and social programs instead of merely language and legalisms of that sort. I suggest that we ought to have known what it is that Quebec wants these powers for, what programs it has in mind-perhaps the other provinces might have agreed, perhaps the federal government might have agreed-and, instead of spend !ng time mainly on constitutional language, discuss the programs that the constitutional language is aimed at. In my view a constitution should not be written in a vacuum. It should arise out of the circumstances and programs and purposes of the nation as a whole.
I want to emphasize on behalf of my party, Mr. Speaker, that the constitutional discussions should continue and that we should realize, as we can realize, the great potentials of this great country.

subtopic: STATEMENT BY PRIME MINISTER ON PROPOSED CHARTER
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the right hon. Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) has just announced that the federal government has accepted the Victoria charter. Any other decision would have astonished me, but he showed some concern that one province, Quebec, vetoed this charter. The question is who said no. I wonder if it was not the Prime Minister himself who vetoed the charter in Victoria by refusing to heed Quebec's requests, specifically as regards section 94A of the constitution.
In any event, Mr. Speaker, it seems to me the problem concerning the proposed charter or the amending formula boils down to a financial issue. The province of Quebec claims power in social security but the federal government refuses. In my opinion, it is not a question of knowing if and how the constitution may be amended, for, if it has already been changed, this can be done again in the future. In fact, one has but to read the sections of the British North America Act to find that, for the past 20, 25 or 30 years, especially as relates to the field of social security, agreements have been made between provinces and the federal government so as to amend the constitution, but that these agreements have always been oriented toward centralization of powers, whereas presently the trend is to decentralization.

June 25, 1971

As for granting powers that provinces are claiming, I must recall that it is not only Quebec that has a bellyfull of centralization by the federal government. Indeed, we hear some pretty strong comments from other provinces, especially from British Columbia, Alberta and Saskatchewan, regarding this.
Thus the province of Quebec must not only claim the power to distribute social security allowances but, at the same time, the financial power to do so. It is well and good to talk about the provinces' self determination but, at the same time, they must be assured of having the power to apply that principle of self determination and I believe that the core of the problem at this time is a financial one.
I feel, Mr. Speaker, that the doors are still open for discussions and negotiations, but the federal government should advise the province of Quebec and all other provinces that it is prepared to yield certain central powers. We have said in the past and again recently that Canada will be a strong country if the provinces are strong and I still believe it. As a matter of fact, I believe we shall have strong provinces if we have strong Canadians inside these provinces.
I think that contrary to what has been understood, the Premier of Quebec has not surrendered to the threat of these Marxists who last Wednesday claimed that should Quebec's answer be affirmative, there would be blood and fire on June 24, a national holiday for French-speaking Canadians. I do not think that this was the case as far as Mr. Bourassa is concerned. I would venture to say that the "No" originated during the Victoria conference.

Mr. Speaker, I request the unanimous consent of the House to propose a motion under Standing Order 43 in a case of urgent and pressing necessity.
This matter concerns the government's reduction of the student militia program which was a tremendous success last year. Over 90 per cent of the 7,850 students who participated in the program and were canvassed thought it worth while and beneficial. Despite these favourable results, the government has cut the program this summer instead of increasing it, as the success of last year's program and continued high student unemployment should dictate. I therefore move, seconded by the hon. member for Vegreville (Mr. Mazankowski):
That this House orders that the Minister of National Defence appear this day before the Standing Committee on External Affairs and National Defence to explain the reduction in this year's expenditures on the student militia program.

speechtext:
In
view of the Prime Minister's statement I think I should ask him whether his statement indicates any change in his position with regard to the deadline for the acceptance of the Victoria charter. Does this mean that the government of Canada is prepared to extend the deadline, and does it mean that, if consent can be achieved from the province of Quebec within what the Prime Minister describes as a reasonable time, the government of Canada will try to reopen the whole question of acceptance?
June 25, 1971

speakeroldname: Right Hon. P. E. Trudeau (Prime Minister):
subsubtopic: EXTENSION OF DEADLINE FOR ACCEPTANCE OF PROPOSED CHARTER
speechtext:
The
answer, Mr. Speaker, is that it does not represent a change in position. The Leader of the Opposition knows that the deadline is not something which was imposed by the federal government on anyone else. It is something that all the first ministers agreed to at Victoria. Indeed, it was made at the request of governments other than the federal government. Our understanding was that, having discussed the matter in February, the first ministers would be able to state their position clearly in Victoria, but some governments requested a delay of ten or 12 days. The federal government agreed to that delay and we gave our answer within that period. There is no change in the federal position on that.
In the hypothetical case where some province might ask for an extension of the deadline, I can only say that I would consult with the other first ministers to see if they want to recognize such a delay. I have no preconceived notion on that, but I do know that it would be reopening the agreement reached at Victoria to have until June 28 to give our answers.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the people of Canada expected the Minister of Finance (Mr. Benson), when he made his budget speech, to answer two important questions which are facing Canadians. First of all, they expected a positive program instead of proposals by the government to deal with the inordinately high rate of unemployment we have at the present time. Second, they expected from the minister some proposals which would begin to implement in Canada an equitable tax system to wipe out the kind of inequities which were dealt with so effectively and in such great detail by the Royal Commission appointed by the former Conservative government, headed by Mr. Kenneth Carter. The minister did not really address himself to either of these questions. On the basis of the minister's speech, the people of Canada must assume that the government has no intention of dealing seriously with either of these problems.
The number of unemployed in Canada in May, as given to the country by the Dominion Bureau of Statistics, was 543,000. The Minister of Finance has taken a great deal of satisfaction from the sharp reduction in the number of unemployed between April and May. If one compares, and one must, the rate of unemployment for May 1971 with May 1970, one can see very quickly that there has been in fact a worsening rather than an improvement in the situation. In May 1970, there were only 513,000 unemployed. In May 1971 30,000 more were unemployed, for a total of 543,000. In May 1970, the seasonally adjusted rate of unemployment, as calculated by the Dominion Bureau of Statistics, was just 5.6 per cent. In May of 1971, it had risen to 6.3 per cent. Indeed, the seasonally adjusted rate used by the government and by the Dominion Bureau of Statistics has not fallen below 6 per cent in any month in the last year, yet the minister has the unmitigated gall to tell the people of Canada the situation is getting better. In May 1971, we

June 25, 1971
The Budget-Mr. Orlikow
had a situation in which 270,000 of our young people between the ages of 14 and 24 were unemployed. We had a situation in which 126,000 people were unemployed for more than six months and in which 112,000 had been unemployed for between four months and six months.
I have one last statistic, Mr. Speaker. In the most prosperous, the largest, province in Canada, the province of Ontario from which the Minister of Finance comes, 5.6 per cent of the labour force, calculated on a seasonally adjusted basis, were unemployed in May. In fact, this year the rate of unemployment in Ontario is higher than it has been for probably ten years, yet the minister tells us things are getting better. Our unemployment is not an accident. The very high percentage of unemployment is part of a deliberate government policy fostered by the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) who, in December 1969, said that in order to meet the threat of inflation he would implement policies of restraint; that he would hold back necessary public works projects, even if this meant an unemployment rate of 6 per cent. Well, we have it. The Deputy Minister of Finance, in a briefing session on the day the minister presented his budget, told the members of the press who were present that to him and to the government full employment meant 5 per cent unemployed.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: I rise on a point of order, Mr. Speaker. I have checked this particular matter with the Deputy Minister of Finance and he assures me that he made no such statement. He merely referred to what had happened over the past 16 or 17 years in Canada.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, today is not the time to talk to the minister about the intemperate speeches of his deputy minister; I can do that on another occasion. Let me say to the Minister of Finance that I was not at the briefing session but I can send the Minister of Finance, if he has not seen these, at least two reports in the newspapers by responsible newspaper reporters and columnists to this effect. So, the deputy minister should watch what he says, because all these reporters did not hear him incorrectly.
The fact is that the kind of unemployment we have is a result of the deliberate policies of this government. This government decided that the increasing cost of living was so serious the economy had to be cooled down. If necessary I can place on the record innumerable speeches by the Minister of Finance, innumerable comments by the Prime Minister, statements by the Prices and Incomes Commission and statements by the Governor of the Bank of Canada, all pointing out the dangers to this country if we did not stop the rising cost of living. The government asked for that advice, but it ignored the advice of virtually every academic economist in this country and for the last 18 months made its first order of business the combatting of inflation. The results were predictable and inevitable.
Canada-and the Minister of Finance has taken great pride in this fact-had probably the lowest rate of increase in the cost of living of any country in the western
world. This rate was less than 2 per cent in 1970. Compared to the countries to which we are often asked to look for a good example, such as West Germany, Japan, France and Great Britain, our increase in the cost of living was very good. However, the results were predictable and inescapable. Along with the United States, we have the highest rate of unemployment of any industrialized country in the western world. In Great Britain, where the Conservative government which was elected a year ago has been following the same kind of policy, unemployment has gone over 3 per cent. The recent local elections in Great Britain resulted in the largest number of losses for a national political party in British local elections. There was a shift of 1,500 or more council seats from the Conservative party to the Labour Party. That Conservative government followed precisely the policy which has been followed by this government.
Now, we are told the government realizes unemployment is important. Now, we are told the government intends to move to deal with unemployment. Now, we are told this expansionary budget will put people back to work. The minister says he is confident the rate of unemployment will drop from month to month in the next year. The figures, however, do not bear out that statement. I have already referred to the figures, but it will take only a few seconds to place them on the record. Let us place on the record the seasonally adjusted figures for Canada since last June. The figure for June was 6.6 per cent, for July 6.7 per cent, for August 6.7 per cent, for September 6.9 per cent, for October 6.6 per cent, for November 6.5 per cent and for December 6.6 per cent. Then we come to this year. For January, 1971 the figure was 6.2 per cent, for February 6.2 per cent, for March 6 per cent, for April 6.7 per cent and for May, the last month for which we have figures, 6.3 per cent.
Where is the reduction about which the minister has been telling the people of Canada for so long? As if that were not bad enough, a couple of days ago during the swing he made through southern Ontario, the Prime Minister again revived the bogeyman that the dangers of inflation were so great the government would have to consider the most drastic kind of measures. I do not know whether he meant price and wage controls or just wage controls, voluntary or by law. If the government intends to deal with inflation as the major thrust in its economic policy, then the people of this country are in for a very serious 12 or 15 months.
When I say that the policies followed by the government will not lead to a solution, certainly not a rapid solution of the problem of the unemployed, the minister can of course say that I am being partisan. If I were to quote economists such as Professor Weldon who was the head of the department of economics at McGill, or Professor Blauer at Brock university, the minister of course would reject the things which they said because they are fairly well known supporters of the party to which I belong. However, I want to quote a few paragraphs from the submission made to the Senate Finance

June 25, 1971

Committee by the Institute for Quantitative Analysis at the University of Toronto, a very highly respected organization whose figures have been used consistently by the minister and the deputy minister in trying to bolster their point of view. Here is what they say, as reported in the Toronto Star issue of June 9, 1971:
The economists predicted that the unemployment rate this year will be higher than last year's 5.9 per cent rate. Unless policies are changed the seasonally adjusted unemployment rate will still be above 6 per cent at the end of the year, they said...
They told the Senate's national finance committee, which yesterday began its six weeks of hearings into ways to improve Canada's economic performance, that the government's policy of "cautious expansion" is not enough to push the unemployment rate down fast enough. A tax cut would help reduce unemployment without bringing on more inflation, they calculated ...
"We believe that there are policy instruments which can be used to move the economy ahead more rapidly while without increasing and perhaps reducing, the rate of price inflation in the short run"...
Either personal income taxes or the federal sales tax should be cut, they said, stating their own preference for a cut in the federal sales tax. Such a cut should cover all federal sales and excise taxes, except the tax on tobacco and alcoholic beverages, and the tax on building materials, they said.
Of course, the minister has done none of the things which were proposed by the Institute for Quantitative Analysis of the University of Toronto.
Now, I want to deal with the second question with which I think the minister should have dealt in his budget speech, namely, the desire of the Canadian people to see a major reform of our taxation system. It was almost 10 years ago that the former prime minister of Canada, the right hon. member for Prince Albert (Mr. Diefenbaker), appointed a royal commission to deal with the question of the inequities in the tax system. We had their report in 1964. Some 18 months later we had a white paper on taxation presented by the minister which indicated a sharp watering down of the proposals made by the Carter Commission. Now, we have the budget and the tax proposals of the minister, which supposedly implement the kind of tax reforms which the people of Canada expected. Do they?
Again, because I do not want the minister to think that this is purely a political and a partisan speech, let me quote just a couple of things said by some people who are not members of our party. Here is what Ronald Anderson, the financial columnist for the Toronto Globe and Mail, said in a column which he wrote on Saturday, June 19 for the Toronto Globe and Mail. I quote just the first couple of paragraphs which read as follows:
The tax bill brought down last night by Finance Minister E. J. Benson represents a major retreat from the proposals advanced in the 1969 white paper on tax reform.
The capitulation, on almost every proposal that had met substantial opposition, was more complete than even the most vigorous critic of the white paper could have foreseen.
All the key proposals-the integration of personal and corporation taxes, taxation of capital gains at full rates, five year revaluation of common shares, and the intended distinction between widely held and closely held corporations-have vanished without a trace, as has the plan to allow small corporations to be taxed as a partnership.
The Budget-Mr. Orlikow
I hope that the hon. member for Grenville-Carleton (Mr. Blair), who gave us a passionate speech the other day in which he said this was the most fundamental change in the tax system that we have had in the last 50 years, is listening. I hope, too, the hon. member for Don Valley (Mr. Kaplan) is listening because he gave us the same kind of nonsensical argument the other day. Here is what the hon. member for Duvernay (Mr. Kierans), the former minister of communications, said in an article which appeared in the Toronto Star on June 21, 1971.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Did you always support him?

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: I support him when he is right, and on this he is right. Let me say to the hon. member in the back row that when the hon. member for Duvernay made a speech, which I hope I will have some time to refer to, on tax policies to the Canadian Economic Association, 300 of the top economists in this country, something unprecedented happened: he received a 12 minute standing ovation. That is a hell of a lot more than the Minister of Finance (Mr. Benson) would get from those people.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
They must have been your party
supporters.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I know that we are growing in strength, but I did not realize that the 300 top economists, academics and business and labour economists, in the country who were attending the Canadian Economic Association meeting were all supporters of the NDP. I did not realize that our support had grown that much.
Let me put on the record one paragraph from the speech by the hon. member for Duvernay. He said:
Except for those whose special position and advantages were being threatened-and isn't that what the commission was all about?-
He was referring to the Carter Commission.
-the report on taxation was universally acclaimed as a model tax system, unique in its attention to fairness. The terms of reference were scrupulously followed while paying full attention to the need to maintain, not increase, government revenues.
Then, in analysing what this budget does, the hon. member for Duvernay said that this budget, and the proposals in the tax bill, simply do not begin to measure up to the principle of equity as expressed either in the Carter Commission report or in the white paper.
What does this budget do, what will it actually mean? I hope the hon. member for Grenville-Carleton, who has some people who are not in the $100,000 a year income bracket in his constituency, will listen to exactly what these proposals do. The tax proposals of this government and of the Minister of Finance mean that an inequitable, regressive and inefficient tax system in Canada with unjust, special privileges existing in many areas will continue as it has for lo, these many years. The proposals fail to shift the basic burden of taxation from those of the lower incomes more proportionately to those at the higher income levels. The federal government is, there-

June 25, 1971
The Budget-Mr. Orlikow
fore, perpetuating the basic defects of the existing tax system, since their tax proposals are not based on the ability to pay, the principle that taxation should be determined by what a person earns and not by how he earns it.
The most astonishing tax proposal by the federal government is the elimination of estate and gift taxes, which will allow wealthy people to pass on from generation to generation their great accumulations of inherited wealth, untouched and intact. For as long as there has been an income tax system in modern industrial countries, a basic principle has been that a good time to begin to redistribute the wealth that people have accumulated is when they die. I am not the greatest defender of the so-called free enterprise system, but I am prepared to argue that one should not stop a person who has intelligence, who is aggressive, who has good ideas and who wants to work hard, from producing wealth and keeping part of it for himself. But surely, Mr. Speaker, we do not want a tax system where not only can a man make a great deal of money by working hard but can turn it over intact to his heirs without paying any tax at all on it.
Let us take the case of a man who accumulates an estate of $1 million. If he has four children, on his death he can turn over $250,000 to each of them. They can invest their $250,000 very conservatively to produce an annual income of between $20,000 to $25,000 a year. They will never have to work a day in their lives. That is the proposal which the Minister of Finance is putting forward in this so-called tax reform bill, and which the hon. member for Grenville-Carleton (Mr. Blair) and the hon. member for Don Valley (Mr. Kaplan) are supporting. Well, Mr. Speaker, they can support it, but the people of Canada sure as hell won't.
Let me deal with some specific illustrations of how these tax proposals will work. Salary and wage earners, including the civil servants whom the hon. member for Grenville-Carleton represents, will be taxed at 100 per cent of their earnings, whether these be the $5,000 which some of the people working in this building make, or the $50,000 which the Deputy Minister of Finance will be making if the Clyne Committee recommendations are implemented. But, Mr. Speaker, capital gains earned by other people, in Ottawa, Toronto or Montreal, will be taxed at only half the amount of those gains. Windfall gains will not be taxed at all. Unemployment insurance benefits and manpower training allowances will be taxable, but business entertainment and related expenses will continue to receive the same favourable treatment as hitherto as deductions from taxable income.
An electrician in Ottawa who must travel to Kingston every day, because that is the only place he is able to get work, will be able to deduct travel expenses. But up to how much, Mr. Speaker? Only up to a maximum of $150. What about the lawyer, the doctor or businessman in Ottawa? Are there any restrictions on what they can deduct for expenses? There are none at all. They will
remain in exactly the same favoured position as that in which they have always been.
The three year tax relief for new co-operatives has been withdrawn, but the business tax credit granted to shareholders is increased from 20 per cent to 33J per cent. That is equity, according to the Minister of Finance.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Now it is taxable; it wasn't before.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
The individual receiving a salary of $100,000 a year will now pay $1,000 less in income tax, compared with a person earning $5,000 in wages, who will save only $14 in tax. But the person earning $11,000 will be paying $78 more under the new proposal. There are a lot of civil servants who make $11,000 a year. Let the hon. member for Grenville-Carleton and the hon. member for Don Valley tell them why they are going to pay more income tax while the man making $100,000 will be paying less. As I have already said, a wage earning employee is limited to $150 in the amount of expenses he can deduct when calculating his income tax, but the high income executive, the type we can see in every expensive and classy hotel, night club and restaurant in every Canadian city will be permitted to deduct expenses in the same generous way as he has always been able to do.
Many Canadians will be paying personal income tax whose incomes are well below the poverty level set out by the Economic Council of Canada, which is $2,000 for a single person and $4,000 for a married couple. But, as I say, an individual will now be permitted to transfer his $1 million estate to his heirs and friends without paying any taxes at all. Of course, the minister will say that he is leaving the field of estate taxes to the provinces. How can you create a more inequitable system than that? How can you create a tax jungle faster than doing just that? Alberta, the province from which the Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance (Mr. Mahoney) comes, has eliminated estate and inheritance taxes. Any person living in Alberta who has $1 million can expect, as long as this government is in power, not to have to pay taxes on the inheritance that he leaves to his children.
I think I have given enough illustrations to make it clear that, while there have been tax changes proposed in the budget and in the tax bills brought forward by the Minister of Finance, there are certainly no tax reforms. If there is any movement towards greater tax equity, more than we have had in the years about which the Carter Commission spoke so eloquently, the rate of that movement is so small it would take the highest powered microscope available in the Dominion of Canada to measure it.
I think that the budget presented on June 18 was a disaster. It was a disaster for those people who are unemployed, the more than half million who are unemployed, and for their families. It was a disaster for every Canadian who, for ten or more years, has been looking forward to real tax reform. Anyone who says that the minister's proposals mean real tax reform is simply not telling the truth. Mr. Speaker, if it were permissible in

June 25, 1971

Parliament to use stronger language, I would say that a person who says this is real tax reform is lying.

speakeroldname: Mr. P. M. Mahoney (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, before starting my comments on the debate as it has progressed up to this point, I should like to pay particular tribute to the members of the Standing Committee on Finance, Trade and Economic Affairs with whom I have had the pleasure of working, not only for the past year but also as a member of the committee during the period when it had the white paper under review. I will particularly express my thanks, and indeed my admiration, to the chairman of that committee the hon. member for Gatineau (Mr. Clermont). I rather doubt that any standing committee of this House has ever been asked to undertake over so long a period of time such a sustained load of work, and to have done it well, and produced a report which very obviously forms a basis of many of the decisions which the government has made in presenting its tax reform legislation. This is indeed an accomplishment for which all members of the committee can take credit, but I must say particularly the chairman, who was responsible for seeing that the work was done well and efficiently.
I had not intended to refer in any detail to the capital gains aspect of the tax reform proposals. However, I could not help but note that the hon. member for Winnipeg North (Mr. Orlikow) made a great deal out of the proposed abolition of the federal estate and gift taxes, without on any occasion mentioning that the capital gains tax proposal involves deemed realization on death.

speakerposition: Chief Government Whip; Whip of the Liberal Party
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: He doesn't understand it.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Perhaps when his favourite newspaper writers deal with that aspect of the legislation he will become more knowledgeable on it. I shall be dealing with the dividend tax credit later in my remarks, but I should note that the hon. member religiously avoided mentioning that while it will be increased to 33 J per cent from 20 per cent, the 33J per cent tax credit will be taxable whereas the present 20 per cent credit is not taxable.
One of the major objectives of tax reform is provincial acceptability. We do not want a tax jungle in Canada, we want a tax system that the provinces can and will use. In two or three weeks time the Minister of Finance (Mr. Benson), together with provincial ministers of finance and provincial treasurers will be meeting in Ottawa to discuss economic affairs, and I suspect that prominent in those discussions will be the new income tax system.
I cannot help but note with a certain degree of nostalgia the passage of the integration proposals of the white paper. It was a system that would have effectively and practically eliminated the double taxation on corporate income as it flowed through to the shareholder. I do not know what the result would have been had opposition to this come only from the corporate community but I think corporate sociologists, writing in the light of
The Budget-Mr. Mahoney
history, may be able to do an interesting case study on the divergence of interest that obviously existed between corporate management on the one hand and corporate shareholders on the other and the attitude of the business community toward integration. It is hypothetical to ask what might have happened had the opposition come only from the corporate side. Some of the provinces, particularly those where corporate activity is the heaviest, waded in in a very emphatic way against integration. In order to try and achieve a system that the provinces can and will use, it was necessary to abandon the proposal in favour of a very much improved dividend tax credit system.
When anybody asks where the money comes from to achieve the things put forward in the new tax proposals, I cannot refrain from mentioning that the estimated cost to the treasury of the integration proposal ranged through $140 million in the first year to $230 million in the fifth year of its operation.
The taxation of capital gains will necessarily reduce savings in the private sector. Experience in other jurisdictions indicates that while the amount available for private investment will be reduced, the capital gains tax in itself is not a disincentive to saving and investment provided the rate is significantly more favourable than that on income. There are also in the new system numerous incentives to encourage increased savings, capital formation and investment.
The new system provides for very important economic objectives, while recognizing the social goal-the need of the individual to provide for his own retirement. I should like to discuss this for a moment or two. There is the increase in limits on contributions to registered pension plans and deferred profit sharing plans to $2,500 and on registered retirement savings plans to $4,000 per year. There is also the increase in the special exemption for older taxpayers to $650 and its extension to all taxpayers age 65 and over, rather than age 70 and over as in the past. Thus, savings for retirement will be encouraged by special tax deductions during the working years and rewarded by a special exemption at the generally accepted retirement age.
The increased limits on contributions to pension, profit sharing and registered retirement savings plans will generate more investment capital, but to assure that this capital will serve Canadian purposes, the plans will themselves be subject to tax unless Canadian investments make up at least 90 per cent of their assets, on the basis of cost. The dividend tax credit, of course, continues to be a major incentive for the Canadian taxpayer to invest in Canada, even though it will no longer be supplemented by the special 4 per cent tax on foreign investment income.
Canadian corporations will be permitted to deduct as an expense the interest on moneys borrowed to purchase shares in other corporations. This will place Canadian companies on as favourable a basis as some foreign companies presently enjoy as a result of their own countries' tax laws. The low rate of tax on corporate earnings will be available only to Canadian owned corporations and

June 25, 1971
The Budget-Mr. Mahoney
will be recoverable if the company passes into foreign hands.
I think we in Canada must appreciate that in encouraging Canadian investment in Canada we cannot dictate to other nations how they will treat their own taxpayers who invest here. How attractive a foreign country makes it to invest here is not only beyond our control, it is irrelevant in terms of our own tax policy. To encourage our own taxpayers we must make it more attractive for them to invest here than elsewhere. We can encourage domestic savings and investment through the tax system but we should not use the tax system as a vehicle to ration capital inflows.
Mr. Speaker, may I call it one o'clock?

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Order, please. It being one o'clock, I now leave the chair.
At one o'clock the House took recess.

AFTER RECESS

The House resumed at 2 p.m.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, when we recessed at one o'clock I was discussing some of the ways in which the tax reform proposals will achieve the express goal of steady economic growth and continuing prosperity. Most wage and salary earners will pay less and thus have more money to spend. There will be some shift in the over-all tax burden, in view of the capital gains tax, to higher taxation of those who are generally believed to save and away from those who are generally believed to spend their extra cash. On the other hand, the progressive reduction of the corporate rates, the elimination of the federal gift and estate taxes, the reduction of the top personal rate by over 20 points, the averaging provisions and the increased incentives to save through pension, profit sharing and retirement savings plans all militate in favour of savings and investment. The new system will leave more money in the hands of all lower income Canadians to spend. It will leave more money in the hands of all married wage earners to spend. It will leave more money in the hands of many of our small, growing corporations. On balance, I am confident that the new system will better serve the goal of steady economic growth and continuing prosperity.
Another goal is equity, or the fair distribution of the tax burden based on ability to pay. The inclusion of the capital gains tax is, of course, one of the major steps towards equity. Also, the changes in personal exemption rates that were last set in 1949 are a major step towards equity. If the $1,000 personal exemption rate was right in 1949, it obviously is not right in 1971. However, Mr. Speaker, this is not simply a matter of applying the increase in the cost of living index to that $1,000 exemption figure and saying that the figure ought to be 170 per cent of what it used to be. The fact is that in the interval
new social programs at the provincial and federal levels, as well as joint programs such as medicare, hospitalization, family allowances and so on, have relieved a great many Canadians, including our low income Canadians, of the need to provide for many of the essential expenses that they had to meet back in 1949.
Accordingly, I contend that the increases in the exemptions are, indeed, sufficient. Without being prodigal, they are certainly fair and equitable in meeting the purposes for which they were designed. We do not cure poverty through the tax system. What the tax system can do is relieve low income Canadians of their tax burden, and I believe the exemption changes achieve a great deal here.
I dealt before lunch with the misleading statements which had been made by the hon. member for Winnipeg North (Mr. Orlikow) who spoke immediately before me. I now wish to deal with some of the statements made by the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Stanfield) in his speech to the House on Wednesday. Some of his objections to the tax reform proposals were as fatuous as those of his hon. friend from Palliser (Mr. Schumacher), who objected to the elimination of the federal gift and estate tax because-and I quote his words from Hansard of June 22 at page 7249-"with the abolition of that tax there will not be any exemption." That is truly a wonderful reason for objecting to the removal of a tax.
One cannot divorce rates from exemptions. They go together. As reported at page 7309, the Leader of the Opposition said:
A person with $1,000 of taxable income who now pays $150 will pay $227.50, and a person with $2,000 of taxable income who now pays $351.50 would pay $474.50.
He followed that with a carefully constructed legalistic argument in which he was talking all the time about taxable income and trying to argue he was not misleading this House and the country by so doing. The Leader of the Opposition talked about the man with a taxable income of $2,000 a year as not having very good entry to the jet set. But who is this man? If he is a married wage-earner with two or three children he will not be the same taxpayer as the taxpayer with $2,000 of taxable income under the existing system. He will be a man earning a gross income of $1,000 more under the new system than under the old. If he is a single wage-earner he will be earning about $600 more under the new system than under the old. If he is a retired pensioner aged between 65 and 70, he will be receiving $1,500 more if married and $1,150 more if single; if he is over 70, $1,000 more if married and $650 more if single.
A man with a taxable income of any given figure under the old system is not in the same position as the man who has the same taxable income under the new system. There is no magic in the tax system. With the changes made, a given amount of taxable income applies to a different and higher total income under the new system. Under the new system, every married taxpayer whose income comes from salary or wages will pay

June 25, 1971

less income tax. Every single taxpayer in similar circumstances will pay less tax if his income is under $8,000. Every retired taxpayer aged between 65 and 69 inclusive will pay less tax whether single or married. Every retired taxpayer over 70 will pay less tax under the new system than under the old system if he is married and less tax as a single taxpayer if his income is less than $8,500. The point which seems to have escaped the Leader of the Opposition, is that taxes are not paid in percentage points but in dollars. The impact of taxation depends not only on the rate of tax levied at a particular level but also on the amount of income which goes untaxed. This is why the increased exemptions must be taken into account along with any changes in rates in order to permit an accurate calculation concerning the effect of the system. A person who today has $1,000 taxable income will not be the same taxpayer who will have $1,000 taxable income under the new system. This is the point the Leader of the Opposition missed.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Shame on old Bob!

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
There are a number of other items designed to bring about greater equity in the business field. The effective elimination of the "incorporated pock-etbook" will be yet another important measure in this field. The term is applied to a situation in which a person, through a corporate fagade, is able to manipulate an investment portfolio so as to take advantage of low rates of corporate tax, tax free passage of dividends from one taxable Canadian corporation to another, the 15 per cent tax on tax paid undistributed surplus and the absence of a capital gains tax, so that he receives investment income on payment of a fraction of the tax he would have paid had he owned the portfolio personally. Along with the capital gains tax and other changes, the denial of the low corporate rate to private companies on portfolio investment income, other than dividends, and the special refundable tax on their portfolio dividend income, will prevent the tax deferral and tax avoidance heretofore favouring the owner of an incorporated pock-etbook as against other taxpayers. Elimination of this loophole is expected to increase revenues by $50 million in the first year of the new system.
Two major changes are proposed affecting the taxation of corporations and their shareholders, each designed to improve the fairness of the system and to encourage economic growth. First, with respect to small business, the present low tax rate of 21 per cent on the first $35,000 of all corporate income is to be replaced by a 25 per cent rate on the first $50,000 of corporate income earned by small corporations which have a need for internally generated capital. This small business incentive will not be available to public or foreign owned or controlled corporations. I regret that no satisfactory way was found of extending this incentive to unincorporated as well as incorporated small businesses. However, from a practical point of view, there are few, if any, businesses likely to need the incentive which do not have the option of incorporation open to them.
The Budget-Mr. Mahoney
A corportation will be considered small until it has accumulated $400,000 of taxable income under the new tax system. As long as its accumulated taxable income is less than $400,000 it may benefit from the low rate. Thus, by paying dividends it may reduce the accumulation and continue its eligibility indefinitely. Earnings in excess of $50,000 in any year would not benefit from the low rate but would, to the extent they are not distributed to the shareholders, constitute accumulated taxable income. Thus a very large private Canadian company would in all likelihood exhaust its eligibility in the first year.
The low rate of tax will be available with respect to business income only-not investment income, except for interest on short term debt securities. Portfolio investment income will be taxed at the full rate in the hands of the company or, if in the form of dividends, at the rate of 33J per cent fully refundable on distribution. It is intended by this system to direct the benefit of the preferential tax rate to small, growing Canadian companies having a bona fide need to generate more of their own capital rather than to their more substantial competitors, and to discourage the build-up of surpluses not needed for business purposes. Since the purpose of this arrangement is to help Canadian businesses, any company which, having benefited from the low rate, passes into non-resident hands, will be required to pay, in addition to regular taxes, the amount of the tax saved.
The other major change is the conversion from the present 20 per cent tax free dividend tax credit to a 33J per cent taxable dividend tax credit. While not achieving the same measure of equity that the abandoned integration system envisaged, it is a substantial improvement on the existing system and goes a long way toward relating the credit for corporation tax paid to the circumstances of the individual shareholder in a progressive income tax system.
The 20 per cent tax free credit increased in value to the shareholder as the shareholder's marginal tax rate increased. The new system will be of the same net benefit as the old to a taxpayer with a 40 per cent marginal tax rate; $11,000 to $14,000 of taxable income under the new system, or, say, $15,000 to $18,000 total income for a married taxpayer with three children under 16-in any case, well into the middle income group. The new rate will be of more net benefit than the old to persons with a lower marginal rate and of less benefit to those with a higher marginal rate. This is not only a major step toward equity in taxation, but it is a major step toward encouraging middle income Canadians to make equity investments.
During the next several weeks tax lawyers, chartered accountants and concerned taxpayers will be studying the bill to ascertain that the amendments do in fact carry out the intention expressed in the budget and as summarized in the summary of 1971 Tax Reform Legislation that hon. members have had delivered to them. We are looking for their help in correcting any errors and noting

June 25, 1971
The Budget-Mr. Mahoney
any omissions, because, notwithstanding the competence of all those from the public service and the advisers from the private sector who assisted in this monumental drafting task, it would be little short of miraculous if there were not some technical errors or omissions.
The budget and summary represent government policy. The government has made the decisions necessary to bring the decade-long tax reform debate to an end. The government will have to account to the electorate for its decisions and for the reformed income tax system.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: You will need a lot of red ink for that.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
That grand old man on the front bench of the Tory party, the hon. member for Prince Edward-Hastings (Mr. Hees), has referred to this as an election budget. I suppose that that is just about the highest compliment that can be paid to any budget. Although it is not an election budget, we on this side of the House would be proud to take it to the electorate if that eventuality occurred.
There is, of course, a body of political thought that denies that the measures constitute reform at all. This view has been expressed by our socialists and their masters in the hierarchy of organized labour. They feel that the white paper was an undesirable retreat from the Carter commission report, and that the new legislation is yet a further retreat from the white paper.
For its part, the official opposition seems, typically, to be riding both sides of the fence. They have not yet decided whether they should claim credit for having "Mau-Maued" the government into an acceptable reform package or whether to attack the package as being neither acceptable nor reform. Having regard to the established speed of their thought processes, we are not likely to learn what the Progressive Conservative position, if any, is going to be in the near future. However, we are learning bit by bit.
My hon. colleague from Don Valley (Mr. Kaplan) noted that these hon. gentlemen had up to Tuesday identified three prongs of their tax reform proposals, namely a 6 per cent across the board tax reduction, tax credits instead of exemptions, and the abolition of the 11 per cent sales tax on building materials. Then, on Wednesday we were pleased to have the leader of the Official Opposition (Mr. Stanfield) disclose two more prongs of the Progressive Conservative tax reform policy. He would not have stuck with the $150 ceiling on employee expense allowances. We do not know how high he would have gone, but he would have gone further than that. Also a Progressive Conservative government would improve child care expense allowances.
At the present time, I am afraid we have to deal with the position taken by the academics and members of the New Democratic Party. They may not like the reform, but that is beside the point. They cannot deny that it is reform. It institutes Canada's first capital gains tax; it abolishes federal gift and estate taxes; it alters fundamentally the basis on which small Canadian corporations
are assisted through the tax system; it changes significantly the way corporations and their shareholders will be taxed; it permits and encourages Canadians to set aside substantially more tax free and low tax dollars for their retirement; and it increases both the number and the effectiveness of incentives to Canadians to invest in and to own Canadian enterprise.
This may not be reform by the standards of the socialists who feel not only that a buck is a buck but that it is the government's buck. It certainly is not revolutionary, but it is reform by any rational standard. It is a reform that is supported by unparalleled research, expert comment and input over a ten-year period. It is a reform founded on an unprecedented process of public participation during the white paper debate-a process of good democracy, good politics and good government. It is, Mr. Speaker, responsible reform.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is a great privilege at this time for me to have the opportunity of speaking in this honourable House. I want to assure all hon. members that, mindful of the important matters embodied in the contents of the budget, and conscious as well that time is a factor, this will not be a long address.
Before speaking in specific terms regarding my constituency, I should like to comment on the administrative changes in the proposed tax reform legislation contained in the budget. I want to commend the minister and the administration for placing the onus of proof on the Crown to establish facts necessary to support a penalty under this legislation. For far too long, the trend has been in the other direction with respect to many different types of legislation, federal and provincial. In my opinion, the government deserves full marks for taking a step in the right direction. I also like some of the other administrative changes made by the minister, but I feel that the change of onus is a fundamental change in principle and one that is long overdue.
The man whom I had the honour to succeed as member for Central Nova, Russ MacEwan, served as a Member of Parliament for 14 years.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Hear, hear.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
May I convey his best wishes to all members of this House and report that he is doing a fine job in his present position as a Judge in the Nova Scotia Magistrates Court. His appointment by the government of Nova Scotia was a fine example of bipartisan support, an appropriate recognition of talent and it was a very popular appointment as well.
My constituency of Central Nova, as most of the cabinet know from personal experience, contains many facets of industry. It is my sincere hope that the interest evidenced in it during the recent byelection by this administration will not wane, and in all seriousness may I say that if the very real needs of Central Nova had been recognized and dealt with on a more consistent and constant basis, and the visits from hon. members of the

June 25, 1971

cabinet had taken place over a longer period of time, then suspicion of pure political expediency as a motive for the attention given to us would not have been so prevalent.
I do not, of course, want to leave the impression that we in Central Nova do not appreciate the attention we received from government, and we hope and trust we will receive further evidence that this government continues to be interested in us. We look forward to many more visits from representatives of this administration to help implement needed changes and improvements.
There have been recent specific moves made by the administration, however, which are causing us in Central Nova real concern. Our Unemployment Insurance Commission facilities in New Glasgow are being partially curtailed. In Stellarton, jobs affecting approximately 20 CNR employees are being phased out. Our freight and passenger service between Pictou and Magdalen Islands is being downgraded. These are truly items of concern, and we want more specific consideration given to the necessity and to the effect of these decisions.
As mentioned before, Central Nova has many types of industry. We have a diversity of interests there, such as coal mining, lumbering, pulp and paper, shipbuilding, steel making, secondary manufacturing, tourism, and service industries, all contributing to the over-all economy. The same may be said, of course, of those engaged in our primary industries of fishing and agriculture. There are many professions and skills employed in the Central Nova economy. Our people deserve to be encouraged. They are industrious, hard working, and want the opportunity of improving their lot and of enjoying a favourable economy in which to build their homes and raise and educate their families. They are true Canadians who want desperately to play their part in building a better country, and who are playing their part even when, at times, the way was made difficult by federal policies which appeared to us rather insensitive.
Those who control the money, control the economy. The government of Canada is clearly in a position to take steps to change its policies, which were admittedly designed to create a certain amount of unemployment, and which caused a great deal of hardship in this nation and discouraged people from pursuing a course of ambitious action. I hope to be able to represent all of the people in Central Nova to the best of whatever ability I possess. In so doing, I solicit the sympathetic co-operation of government and, if I may, I would like therefore to draw a few items of importance to the attention of government at this time.
The question of off-shore mineral rights is of vital concern to all Nova Scotians, Mr. Speaker. I find it hard to accept any proposition that the provinces must be subservient to the Federal Government in this regard. Rather, I feel that the primary benefits, the lion's share if you will, should belong to the provinces-that the provincial rights in regard to potential revenues from off-shore mineral and oil reserves be paramount.
The Budget-Mr. MacKay
On Friday, a week ago, the right hon. Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) stated in this House that the Federal government was still awaiting from the provinces answers to the plan that was put to them more than a year ago. To me, as a Nova Scotian, this is rather disheartening. I think that our province should have by this time made its recent position clear. Having said this, Mr. Speaker, one can hardly blame the Federal government if its proposals, put forth some time ago, have not yet been answered, if there has been no dialogue because of delay by the provinces. And in this regard I am thinking particularly of Nova Scotia. Whatever the cause of delay, whether it be federal or provincial, I would earnestly request the hon. Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Greene), as well as any other members of the administration who have direct or indirect responsibility in this regard, to expedite immediate consideration of this important matter.
Agriculture in Central Nova consists principally of mixed farming. The farmers are, for most part, engaged in farming in a small way, but one of their big concerns is poor markets for their produce. They are very disturbed about the implications and possible effects of Bill C-176.
The regimentation which is implicit in this piece of legislation causes them misgivings. Our farmers are also conscious that they have a weak, or if you prefer, a small market base in their own native province. They realize that it is imperative that their produce have free access to markets in other provinces, particularly in central Canada. Bill C-176 does nothing to guarantee any such access, and I would urge this government to consider this particular point. The marketing board which, as I understand it, will be created when this bill becomes law, purports to represent both producers and consumers. It seems to me that this is a difficult task for one board to do as it represents a built-in conflict of interest.
In passing, I would like to comment that I have not as yet seen in the information surrounding the budget any estimate of how much, if any, extra revenue farmers will contribute in taxes to the federal treasury as a result of changes in rules relating to the depreciation of their equipment, etc. I think this will be of interest to hon. members of the House when it becomes available.
The ferry service between Caribou, Nova Scotia, and Wood Islands, Prince Edward Island, is a vital link between these two provinces, and another ferry is presently under construction by the Ferguson Industries at Pictou. But, when this vessel is complete, which will not be for some time, yet another is required to take care of the congestion which, during the height of the tourist season, presents serious problems. Now is the time for the government to take steps in this regard. Better installations and arrangements are required to expedite the freight and passenger service between Pictou and the Magdalen Islands.
Another matter of urgent concern is that when the new Michelin Tire plant gets into production there will be a problem in respect of increased requirements necessary to expedite transportation in the Port of Pictou, and

June 25, 1971
The Budget-Mr. MacKay
urgent consideration should be given to establishing rollon and roll-off wharf facilities there or there will be further difficulties.
As far as the fishing industry is concerned in my constituency, one of the things that is required is better bait freezing and storage facilities along the east shore of my constituency in the Sheet Harbour area. The Minister of Fisheries, now of Environment (Mr. Davis), I had been informed, has been to the area at least on one occasion, accompanied by the Minister of Highways of the province of Nova Scotia, as he now is, and is well aware of the problems involved when fishermen have to sell bait fish for a small price and buy them back at a much higher price when needed, simply because they have no way of preserving them during the interim. As far as I know, nothing has been done in this regard.
Fishermen require more efficient facilities for wharves in our constituency. There is a need for improved lighting, and in some cases for improved hoisting devices, so that fishermen can use these wharves to the best advantage. These are not extravagant things which we are requesting, but things that could be done at a minimum of expense which would make life a lot easier for these people who have to use these facilities.
The problem of McBain Mine in the Thorburn area is one which this government has recognized and dealt with to some considerable extent. There is a feeling, however, that although the $750,000 allocated to keep the mine in operation is a worthwhile step, there still must be a decision made and communicated to those most concerned about the basic policies involved in the ultimate future of this mine. I suggest that if the McBain Mine, which appears to be basically a good one, is to be kept in operation, development work must be undertaken at once to open another wall or face. If the mine is definitely to be phased out, so that this course of action would not be practical, then it is time the miners knew, so that some of them at least could make other arrangements as individual opportunities become available. I would ask the government to remember, however, that these men like mining coal. They are proud of their work and proud of their fellow miners. They have a team spirit and they want to make a success of the McBain operation. This is also true of the Drummond, the other mine in Pictou County. So, these miners should be told what the future holds for them now, not when we are in the midst of another election campaign.
It should also be noted that coal is still a factor in considering fuel reserves and requirements, and it would be very difficult at a future date to replace the expertise of these miners and management if it became necessary to consider mining coal again in volume in Pictou County.
The situation as far as minority groups are concerned in my constituency can certainly be improved with help from this administration. Federal moneys, I am sure, can be found to assist in upgrading living conditions for our black people. Many of them, Mr. Speaker, need extra assistance in order to upgrade their position in society.
By a joint effort with local government, the federal authorities can remedy a crying need.
Our Indian people are likewise not satisfied with their living conditions. The hon. Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development (Mr. Chretien) might be so kind as to have some of his staff check into the general situation at Boat Harbour to see if some extra funds can be allocated to improve the adverse conditions created by the Boat Harbour pollutants. These pollutants have had several side effects directly affecting the people living nearby on the Pictou Landing Indian Reserve.
I believe it is correct to say that the provincial government, as compensation to the Department of Indian Affairs and Northern Development for the land expropriated and the other adverse conditions created, paid a fairly large sum of money to the Federal Government at the time the Boat Harbour project was being initiated. It seems only fair that some of this money at least should be directly distributed to the people affected by it, and on whose behalf it was paid. I respectfully urge the minister to look into this matter at his early convenience.
The problems of unemployment have affected many of our people. This situation has not been to the liking of government, I fully realize, but it was this government which, as a necessary evil in their opinion, initiated policies to combat inflation which directly caused it. People in this country must not be deprived of employment in such a calculated manner, even if the excuse is to cure the disease of inflation, because, Mr. Speaker, such a cure, in my humble opinion, is worse than the original disease.
I believe it was H. L. Mencken who once said, in his inimitable style, that "Democracy is what most people want, and they deserve to get it-good and hard!" But this is not the type of democracy that this country, the Atlantic region, and especially Cenral Nova, wants if one equates democracy with hardness in the sense that it is hard to get a job, hard to make a living, etc. In fact, hard times in the Maritimes is a cruel catch phrase for those of us who live there, who really care, and who, like all other Canadians, want to progress.
Problems relating to pollution are all too familiar in Central Nova. Whether the cause be effluents from pulp-mills, fish processing plants, or emissions from industrial smoke stacks, the effect is the same-damage to the ecology and restrictions in the use and enjoyment of our environment. We have flowing through our most populous area a very scenic and potentially useful river known as the East River of Pictou. This river could be of great benefit to the citizens in the immediate area and a great asset in many ways, but now its main use is as an open sewer, at least until one reaches a point several miles from its mouth. The widely publicized pollution of Boat Harbour and the Northumberland Strait is another sore point among the people concerned with our environment in Central Nova. We are looking hopefully to the government to implement some of the provisions of the Canada Water Act and thus, in co-operation with the

June 25, 1971

other levels of government concerned, take some protective and remedial action.
On the subject of forestry, Central Nova contains hundreds of thousands of acres of forests, some of which are of little value because of poor cutting practices followed in the past and, may I say, in some cases continuing. There has been pitifully little reforestation done and, while the Provincial Department of Lands and Forests is primarily responsible in this field of endeavour, I am sure there is a need for federal participation and technical assistance in keeping with a national forest policy.
Not only in Central Nova, but all across the nation, forestry is a mainstay of economic wellbeing. In the Atlantic region, forest products provide an economic lift in excess of $100 million each year. Besides this direct benefit, there are related effects in transportation, sales and processing. Some concerned organizations, like the Maritime Lumber Bureau, have claimed that since 1949 progressively inflated costs of production in the forest industry have amounted to 40 per cent. I, personally, feel that this figure is too low. While the industry has been able to absorb most of these costs in different ways, such as new manufacturing uses of waste products and more efficient cutting, the more efficient methods of cutting and harvesting trees have had a terrible effect on the woodlands themselves. Under so-called new and modern harvesting methods the areas involved are often totally devasted. I suggest, Mr. Speaker, that this very important primary industry and natural resource must be developed. At the same time, however, it must be protected and there is a definite role for the federal government to play in supervising the preservation of this nation's forests.
Some relief has, in fact been given in the last budget to the forest industry in that certain types of duties on imported equipment have been removed and fuel oil has been made slightly cheaper. However, the 11 per cent federal sales tax still remains and this is a real and continuing impediment to the forest industry, certainly in our area.
Education is a topic of universal interest and concern in my constituency. Central Nova is certainly not unique in having problems relating to high property taxes resulting from the escalating cost of education. Nova Scotia, generally, has always had an excellent reputation in the field of education. Many students come to our province from all parts of Canada to be educated, and not only on the postgraduate level. I think it is fair comment that our province has on balance contributed a great deal to Canada in sending well educated persons all over this country.
