We recognize that the federal government is making an increasing contribution to the costs of education in our province. Participation in the fields of post secondary education programs and on other levels as well, such as vocational training programs, has been in effect for some time and has been welcomed. We ask that these policies be continued and escalated so that our high standards can be maintained without imposing a crushing burden on property owners.
Although the area of Central Nova is a designated one, as is all of Nova Scotia, the incidence of industrial
The Budget-Mr. Clermont
expansion has been rather slow, except possibly in a few selective areas. Moreover almost none of that expansion can be attributed to the Department of Regional Economic Expansion.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Hear, hear.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
In fairness, however, it must be pointed out that the Department of Regional Economic Expansion has given a grant under its Regional Development Incentives Act to the Trenton Steel Works at Trenton. This grant for modernization amounted to $569,364. The total approved capital cost for that modernization of the Trenton Steel Works was $2,846,824. What is required, Mr. Speaker, is more grants of this nature and, at this point, the entire region should, I suggest with deference, be classed as a growth area under the required designation of the Department of Regional Economic Expansion so that we could enjoy the special benefits implicit in that type of classification.
Pictou County, like Sydney, is one of the traditional areas where manufacturing and mining have always taken place in Nova Scotia, and we need all of the assistance possible in order to maintain the gains that have been made in recent years. The Scott Paper complex, which has been in operation since 1967, unfortunately was not eligible for regional development incentive grants because at that time regional development incentive assistance was not available to primary producers. However, I would hope, as I say, that the government would consider taking steps to recognize our special needs in the constituency in this regard.
Perhaps before closing, Mr. Speaker, I might again make reference to the recent campaign in Central Nova in the spirit of traditional Nova Scotian political competitiveness. I should like to say with all deference to the President of the Privy Council (Mr. MacEachen) that he should not worry so much in future about the people of Nova Scotia sending one more Tory to Ottawa, as he admonished them not to do, but that in future he should worry rather about the very real possibility of them sending one less Liberal.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, at the outset, I would like to acquaint hon. members and the public with the work done by the Finance, Trade and Economic Affairs Committee when it studied the proposals for fiscal reform.
The document was referred to the Committee on December 19, 1969, and the same day, a press release invited taxpayers to send us their briefs and comments on the subject. In all, we received 524 briefs, as well as 1,093 letters and other evidence.
The first public meeting was held on January 15, 1970, the witnesses being the hon. Minister of Finance (Mr. Benson) and a group of officials from his department. The closing session was a public meeting with the hon. Minister of Finance held on August 4, 1970.

June 25, 1971
The Budget-Mr. Clermont
During the study, the Committee met 146 times and examined 211 briefs submitted by 820 persons. In addition to the briefs presented during its hearings, the committee studied many other written briefs.
pjn.)
The committee sat in Ottawa for two weeks in July- during the summer recess-and then toured Canada from the Atlantic to the Pacific in the first week in August to hear the public, the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. Gray) and the Minister of Finance. It also sat in Ottawa during the first two weeks in September to draft the report tabled in the House on October 5, 1970.
I must point out that the members did not receive any additional remuneration for attending the sittings of the committee during the summer recess, nor any allowance for their expenses for food and lodging while they sat in Ottawa. This gives you an idea of the tremendous amount of work the members of the committee did. As chairman, I take this opportunity to thank them for their co-operation, at all times, and to thank the staff of the committee, the members of the translation and interpretation services, the tax experts and the civil servants of the various departments.
Now, I would like to comment a little on the tax reform legislation and on the budget. In some quarters, Mr. Speaker, they claim this reform, as regards income tax, is weak and incomplete since it does not deal with all the reforms recommended by the Royal Commission on Taxation, particularly on sales and excise taxes. However, I think that the income tax changes have been closely studied. I would like to quote in this connection an excerpt from an editorial published on June 21, 1971 and signed by Mr. Claude Lemelin, editorialist at Le Devoir, who has not always been tender toward the monetary and financial policies of the Minister of Finance. Here it is:
But it is mostly the fiscal reform stated to come into force on January 1, 1972 which should retain the taxpayers' interest. This reform is so far-reaching-
I repeat, Mr. Speaker,
-so far-reaching that its analysis is impossible in one single stage.
Here is another excerpt from an article published by the Ottawa Citizen on June 19, 1971. It was written by Charles Lynch, chief of Southam News Services. I quote: [English]
It is a massive achievement, offering a nice balance of logic, efficiency and political appeal, both long and short term.

Further on he says:

There is an emphasis on people throughout the massive budget papers, and Mr. Benson manages to sound as though he cares for low-income, middle-income and high-income Canadians in equal measure...
His tax reforms are not so extreme as business and industry had feared, or as the Royal Commission on Taxation, chaired by Kenneth Carter, had hoped.
The Carter recommendations were too sweeping to be practical in a stable society.
The white paper proposals were too tough to be acceptable. [Translation]
To all those who complain that the reform is incomplete, I answer by saying that the Commission recommended amendments to the Income Tax Act, to the Estate Tax Act and to the Excise Tax Act. As far as the recommendations having regard to fiscal reform are concerned, first reading of a bill will be moved on Wednesday, June 30, 1971.
In 1968, the federal legislation on gifts and estates was amended, and it will be abolished on December 31, 1971, if Parliament accepts the changes recommended by the Minister of Finance.
Besides, the Minister of Finance recently suggested that the following step would be related to sales and excise taxes.
Mr. Speaker, I think that two hits out of three is a pretty good score.
I should like to deal with another aspect of tax reform, namely, the participation of the public in the development of this reform. I read in the June 17, 1971 issue of the Montreal La Presse an article based on a Canadian Press release, in which I noted the following two sentences which I quote:
The first outcome of the major experience gained by the Trudeau government in participatory democracy will be realized tomorrow as a piece of legislation to change the income tax system.
When the government published its famous white paper on tax reform on November 7, 1969, inviting the public to express criticisms of its contents, he aimed at starting a heated debate on the pros and cons.
Doubts and criticisms have been voiced on this type of participation. It was alleged that the Government was not serious in calling for these contributions and that the decision to entrench the White Paper proposals in a new legislation had already been taken. Some even suggested that the relevant bill had been printed, although the Right Honourable Prime minister (Mr. Trudeau) or the Minister of Finance had repeatedly given assurances to the contrary.
I would like to refer to paragraph 1.1, Chapter I, at page 5 of the White Paper which reads:
In this White Paper the Government of Canada places before Parliament, the Canadian people and the provincial governments its major proposals for reform of the income tax structure. The government wil welcome public discussion of the proposals, particularly in the parliamentary committee considering them. Detailed discussions are also planned with provincial government representatives.
Another quotation, this one from the hon. Minister of Finance (Mr. Benson) from a speech he made at a public meeting in Montreal on March the 8th, 1968:
The government has started the debate on tax reform with the White Paper announcing our proposals, and I insist on the word "proposals", because we were aware of the fact that we did not know all the answers to prepare the best tax system possible for the country. The government was sure

June 25, 1971

Canadians could be counted on to examine and comment on these proposals in a reasonable way. There was a little hysteria and some exaggerated and fallacious publicity in the headlines. But we also received many judicious letters, full of good ideas from individuals. We will examine them when we come to the briefs presented to the parliamentary committees and the conclusions of these committees. One of the most encouraging aspects of the debate, and this proves that the White Paper process is a useful one, is the number of letters indicating that their authors had taken time to think about our proposals and were trying to submit ideas to improve or modify the White Paper.
To those who still have doubts I suggest they read, if they have not already done so, the reports of the Senate and House of Commons committees. They will see if that kind of participation produced tangible results. Furthermore, the hon. member for Edmonton West (Mr. Lambert) in his television comments on the budget last Friday is reported to have said that at least two thirds of the recommendations included in the report of the House of Commons committee had been included in the tax reform.
Another criticism we hear about public participation is that the witnesses who appeared before the committee were there to defend vested rights. This is undoubtedly partially true, but those people should tell us whether they consider as being on the same level the representatives of the following organizations, who appeared before the committee: The Canadian Bankers' Association, The Canadian Pulp and Paper Producers' Association, The Canadian Manufacturers' Association, the Rio-Tinto Zinc Corporation Ltd., the Canadian Bar Association, the Canadian Construction Association, the Canadian Medical Association, the Public Service Alliance of Canada, The Saskatchewan Wheat Pool Employees Association, The Canadian Labour Congress, The Canadian Federation of Agriculture, The National Cancer Institute, The Family Vanier Institute, The National Farmers' Union, the Ontario Government, the Saskatchewan government and the Canadian Welfare Assistants Association.
Mr. Chairman, my remarks will now deal for a few minutes with the tax reform as concerns personal and corporations income tax and capital gains tax.
Many changes concerning the personal income tax are included in the bill tabled last Friday and I should like to indicate a few of them.
First, the $1,000 basic exemption was increased to $1,500 for single people, which represents a 50 per cent increase. Moreover, married people will get a $2,850 exemption instead of $2,000, which represents an increase of 42.5 per cent. A special annual $650 exemption, instead of $500, was granted persons of 65 or over, contrarily to the present system which helps only people of 70 or more.
This innovation as well the income supplement exemption, as of January 1, 1971, will be welcomed by old age pensioners and guaranteed income supplement recipients.
The Budget-Mr. Clermont
Blind persons and disabled persons confined to a bed or a wheelchair will also be entitled to special yearly deduction of $650 instead of $500.
Secondly, when two married people are working or when only one working parent is left in the family, the bill provides for the deduction of child, care expenses up to $500 per child under 14. This benefit also applies to older children mentally retarded or physically handicapped, with a ceiling of $2,000 per family, however.
Thirdly, further changes are recommended in the bill with regard to the travelling expenses of workers, medical expenses and charitable donations, the limit on which is increased to 20 per cent of the taxpayer's income from the existing limit of 10 per cent.
Salaried people will also be able to deduct their professional expenses up to 3 per cent of their employment income, with a yearly maximum of $150 and without a voucher being required. Certain moving expenses may also be deducted from income when the taxpayer moves to a new job.
As of July 1, 1971, the 3 per cent surtax will be removed and taxpayers with a taxable income under $500 will be tax exempt.
A highly controversial white paper proposal recommended the removal of the 21 per cent tax rate on the first $35,000 of corporation profits. The committee received many briefs asking that this low tax rate be maintained at least for small corporations. A number of suggestions were put forward but the problem was to define a small corporation. I welcome the proposal whereby 25 per cent of the first $50,000 of Canadian-owned private corporations income are not taxable. The government also found a formula defining small and medium businesses, that is a taxable income of up to $400,000. Thereafter the low tax rate no longer applies.
Similarly, the income to which the low rate applies must be reinvested in the company or paid to shareholders as taxable dividends. Otherwise, the benefit of the low rate will be curtailed. This is why I would have some reservations on that amount of $400,000, were not those conditions mandatory.
Another proposal that was much questioned is taxation of capital gains. Considerable reservations and earnest objections were raised on the taxation of capital gains deriving from the sale of principal residence, personal property, deemed benefits on a five year basis of widely-held corporations, and so forth.
Among the reasons given for not considering capital gains as income, was that Canada was a young country and would need all its capital. Moreover, this additional taxation would reduce savings and eliminate the risk feature.
Mr. Speaker, as the study was progressing, I felt among the witnesses the conviction that following the tax reform the capital gains would be considered as income, and some apprehension of the rules that would govern them.

June 25, 1971
The Budget-Mr. Clermont
Here is what Mr. Christopher Young, editor of The Ottawa Citizen, had to say in an article on capital gains that was published on June 17, 1971:

In terms of fundamental reform, the greatest change is the capital gains tax. Few could seriously argue that it has been fair to allow money earned from the appreciation of capital assets to go untaxed while money earned by sweat or by hard brain-twisting was assessed at ever heavier rates. Rather the argument was that a capital gains tax would inhibit the growth of an underdeveloped economy.
That position has been dubious for many years and has now been finally abandoned. To this extent, the philosophy of the Carter commission that "a buck is a buck" has been accepted, even though the impact of the new tax has been softened for both administrative and political reasons.

I consider that the Minister of Finance proposed an acceptable policy when he recommended adopting a general rule whereby 50 per cent of capital gains will be included in income, taxed at regular rates for personal or corporate income tax; allowing taxpayers to deduct 50 per cent of capital losses from half of capital gains; waiving tax on the sale of a principal residence together with one acre of land; making gains subject to taxation and losses deductible when a taxpayer sells property, makes a gift of it, or leaves it in his estate upon his death; deferring capital gains in case of gifts or bequests between spouses; and, because of deemed realization at death, abolishing federal taxes as from December 31, 1971 on estates and gifts.
I should now like to discuss budget provisions which will further facilitate our economic development which started over 18 months ago through various provisions such as, in the field of monetary policy, a considerable increase of the money supply, which has been felt since last spring. This increase resulted in a considerable decrease of interest rates, including the prime rate of chartered banks, and mortgage rates.
Between last April and February of the present year, there have been six successive reductions of the Bank of Canada discount rate bringing the 8.5 per cent rate back to 6.5 per cent. The interest rate on long term government bonds has decreased from 8.3 per cent early in 1970 to 6.85 per cent in February 1971, in the field of fiscal and financial policies. The hon. Minister of Finances introduced in his budget speech of December 3, 1970 new programs featuring additional incentives to help people, areas and industries affected by the slowing economic growth.
Let me point out a few: a 10 per cent increase in unemployment insurance benefit, until the coming into effect of the new program on July 1, 1971; a $23 million program designed to improve public buildings in areas severely hit by unemployment; a program through which $20 million were earmarked for the construction of roads and the development of services at the Montreal International Airport; funds to the Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation; a special loan program whereby an
amount of $160 million was provided for undertaking immediate labour intensive projects.
In the field of social security, the increase in the guaranteed income supplement came into effect on April 1, 1971. This increase has raised by almost $200 million the benefits to persons who receive this supplement.
In his budget speech last Friday, the Minister of Finance proposed policies to maintain and further economic expansion. The 3 per cent surtax on personal and corporate income tax is abolished as of July 1, 1971. The 12 per cent sales tax will be removed as of now from all anti-pollution equipment. This exemption will apply to all machinery and apparatus bought by manufacturers and producers for the detection, prevention, elimination and reduction of water, soil and air pollution.
The duty-free entry of production machinery not available in Canada and considered to be in the public interest will extend to sawmills and logging operations in order to help the lumber industry. The suspension for a period of two years of the J of a cent per gallon duty on heavy fuel oils will help offset sizeable price increases incurred by pulp and paper producers and power utilities. The last three measures will serve as an incentive to the pulp and paper industry which is now facing a very delicate situation involving several thousands of plant and bush workers and, in many instances, farmers.
The immediate elimination of the 15 per cent excise tax on recreational equipment such as television sets, radios and high-fidelity systems will no doubt relieve consumers in an area which has greatly suffered from the recent economic situation.
In concluding, Mr. Speaker, I would like to call the attention of the government and especially that of the hon. Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce (Mr. Pepin) who, I believe, will be travelling to China from June 25 to July 4. He will be accompanied by a delegation of federal and provincial government officials and by representatives from the private sector, one of them being delegated by the pulp and paper industry, and I hope the party will meet with people who will be interested in purchasing pulp and paper products.
It is well known, Mr. Speaker, that the pulp and paper industry has been experiencing difficulties for some time. Several explanations are put forward, but it seems to me that our decreasing exports are one of the main reasons. Our exports to the United States have diminished by more than 5 per cent during the first four months of this year and we are well aware of the significance of our exports, especially when in the province of Quebec 72 per cent of that production goes abroad. Our exports to Europe have decreased by 19 per cent during the same period.
I hope that this delegation will do its utmost to interest the Chinese in buying our pulp and paper products, thus enabling the workers in that industry to view the future with more confidence, because I know that on a few occasions since January 1, 1970, in various industries throughout Quebec-and I believe that the same situation prevails in other provinces-some workers have been

June 25, 1971

asked to stay away from work for one or two weeks. I hope that this delegation will be in a position to bring back good news to the pulp and paper industry.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the budget speech on June 18 brought but very minor tax relief. The Minister of Finance (Mr. Benson) obviously wanted to have it both ways.
The basic income tax exemption, as proposed, does not meet the requirements of the cost of living which increased constantly since the last war, and nothing indicates that this will stop since solutions tried by governments are the same which have generated this inflationary run.
The poor who make up one third of the people have little hope, and each budget and each session leave them more deceived.
The minister has announced the elimination of the 12 per cent sale tax on margarine. Yet, I have heard no cry of joy from the dairy producers, especially those from the east. The margarine trust is more powerful and, no doubt, contributes more to election funds.
The hon. minister also announced the removal of the 15 per cent excise tax on television sets, radios and high fidelity equipment. This is all very well for those who can afford them. I think however that it would have been preferable to make it possible for low income families to have a house of their own.
The budget statement does not make many proposals on housing. The sales tax on building materials should have been repealed in the first place. Indeed, in my opinion-and this opinion is shared by my colleagues of the Social Credit-our principle should be: to each family its own house. It has been found in many walks of our society that a high number of our Canadian families, because of a clearly inadequate income, cannot have decent housing and have to live in chicken coops and pay inflated rents. When I say chicken coops, Mr. Speaker, I refer to high-rise buildings where people must live, without sun, space or fresh air. Those public housing projects are not suitable for human beings, who are not meant to be fattened and slaughtered like poultry. On the contrary, everywhere where such chicken coops have been built, the children's health was found to be worse than elsewhere, because they don't get any sun, exrcise or fresh air. In multiple housing, the mothers' health is affected and, according to recent surveys, the suicide rate is the highest there, due to nervous breakdowns.
Mr. Speaker, the federal government is primarily responsible for our banking system and our monetary and tax policies. Therefore, it should see to it that each family has a house to live in. To achieve this purpose, it must first of all abolish the 11 per cent sales tax on building materials.
The Minister of Regional Economic Expansion (Mr. Marchand) is distributing here and there some rather important subsidies for the construction of sawmills specifically designed for building materials. However, the Minister of Finance is levying an 11 per cent tax on
The Budget-Mr. Laprise
those building materials thus preventing the consumers, workers and family heads to purchase a house, because that 11 per cent tax considerably increases the cost of housing and the down payment on a house is higher. So low income people-those we have been trying to help in the last few months-find it difficult to buy a house even though the interest rates on loans have been somewhat reduced.
And at this stage, Mr Speaker, I would like to say that when a small wage earner applies for a loan either with Central Mortgage & Housing Corporation or with an authorized lender, he commits himself, as everybody else, to pay a rather high interest for 20, 25 or even 35 years, not only on the price of the house, but also on the 11 per cent tax on building materials. So it is obvious that this 11 per cent tax cripples the construction industry. In fact, its removal should have been a priority in the budget brought down by the Minister of Finance.

There is no mention in either the budget speech or the tax proposals of that 11 p. 100 tax.
Moreover, a fund should be set up to provide for the housing needs of everyone and especially the low income groups. Low interest bearing loans should be granted to those wishing to buy their own home. The present rate of interest for people earning up to $6000 a year is 7J p. 100. This is a lower rate than for other loans, but then again, Mr. Speaker, it is clear that for those with a yearly income of $4,000 to $6,000, that rate is still too high and requires them to make large payments.
The Minister without Portfolio responsible for housing (Mr. Andras), has announced, some time ago, that p. 100 loans would be granted to those earning less than $6,000 a year. As can be seen, poor people as always, are looked after last. But they also have to contend with a shortage of funds and red tape.
The cost allowed for a single dwelling is so low, taking into account the requirements like salaries, taxes and charges for services, that contractors almost have to build rows of poor quality houses. A few weeks ago I visited a housing development in Pointe-Gatineau and I was scandalized to see the kind of shacks that had been built there during the winter. Five years from now, these houses will be in a worse state than those they have replaced. Worst of all, the municipalities are now objecting to the construction of low-cost housing.
The mayor of Laval, Mr. Jacques Tetreault, stated recently that this low-cost housing program is not viable for municipalities because the cost for installing the infrastructure, that is drains, sewers, water lines, streets and lighting, is higher than the revenue in taxes from theses houses. Many municipalities prefer $30,000 to $50,000 houses to $11,000 or $12,000 houses for construction. That is obvious since the tax rate is much higher and the services required are much greater. So, the municipalities obviously prefer that houses worth $50,000

June 25, 1971
The Budget-Mr. Laprise
be built, rather than $11,000, $12,000 or $15,000 houses, as is intended for low income groups. According to the mayor of Laval, the infrastructure for multiple dwellings is less expensive because they can shelter more families in less space.
This is why they recommend building those high-rise chicken coops to accommodate low-income families, which only deprives them of space and fresh air. It must be recognized that a family which lives in its own house is in a better position to educate its children. For instance, if I own a garden, a lawn, flowers, I must see that my children do not destroy these flowers and this garden. If I bring up my children in such conditions, I am almost sure that they will not destroy the neighbour's garden or flowers. But if the children do not know what planting and cultivating a flower means, they do not know its value and they destroy the neighbour's, because they have not had the proper education.
Low-income families cannot own their homes because the municipalities cannot balance their expenditures and revenue.
Mr. Speaker, we all know in what situation municipalities are now because of the high cost of credit.
The Laval mayor added that the substructure to allow
for the construction of 128 new houses would cost $287,880; that $37,425 would have to be paid annually to reimburse capital and interest, that is a total of $748,508 or $460,925 in interest, in other words almost twice the amount of the $287,880 loan.
This means that under the present system, to plan for the construction of 128 homes in Laval for low-income families, the municipality would have to pay financiers $460,925 over the next twenty years. A system that forces a municipality to pay double the value of the services it must provide for 128 low rent housing units is ridiculous. Meanwhile, people with low income will have to pay back twice or three times the price of their houses.
That is surely profitable for lenders or financiers, but I think the population, not the financiers, should get the most out of it. That is why the Social Credit has been urging the government for a long time to grant interest-free loans to municipalities, particularly when the minister in charge of housing has obtained from the cabinet permission to make funds available to building contractors for houses designed for low-income families.
The minister should have obtained at the same time permiss on to make interest-free loans to municipalities that will have to provide services and a substructure for construction, at least for new developments.
The municipalities would not have had any reason for complaining in this respect about the program proposed by the minister responsible for housing. They would rather have fully accepted this program, but on account of the expenses in which the municipalities are thereby involved, it happens that quite a number of them are concerned because these expenses will have to be borne out by other homeowners.
Sometime ago, the Canadian Federation of Mayors and Municipalities submitted a brief to the government and, among other things, they said and I quote:
Be it resolved that the Federal and Provincial Governments be asked to undertake, after consultation with the municipal associations, the establishment of a specialized municipal credit institution or institutions to facilitate municipal borrowing for capital works.
It is made quite clear in the Minister's response that the Federal Government rejects the Resolution and is not interested in pursuing the matter any further. Unfortunately this constitutes a rejection of the principle of tri level co-operation in the most important area after taxation. We recognize, and it is recorded in the resolution, where Local Government sits in relation to the Federal Government. We are forced to ask whether the Federal Government is justified in rejecting our suggestions in the manner that has become traditional. Further, we are forced to ask how the Federal Government can reconcile the creation of a Ministry of Urban Affairs through which it "seeks, by making rational efforts in these fields, and through consultation with those most directly concerned, to help Canadians reach and implement the decision that will determine their urban future" with its rejection of tri level co-operation in the area of capital financing.
I continue the quotation.
We ask as well how the Federal Government can extend interest free lending privileges to under developed nations while refusing to extend those same privileges to underprivileged municipalities that are so numerous in Canada.
Mr. Speaker, this quotation speaks by itself.
Considering the great number of low income families that do not own a home, one realizes that this is to the advantage of slum owners in the province of Quebec. The government decided last year and again this year to grant further subsidies for the building of homes for low income people.
As I said a while ago, municipalities have to cope with financial problems. As a matter of fact, I know that in some cases especially in Quebec, 50 per cent of their budget goes to pay the interest on the municipal debt. In such conditions, they can no longer look after development especially housing development. That is why we are justified in calling for interest-free loans to municipalities so that they may set up the infrastructures required for housing development.
Secondly,-and the Minister of Finance should have mentioned it in his speech last Friday-we call for the removal of the 11 per cent sales tax on building materials since, by encouraging the construction industry, we would fight unemployment. Moreover, as a result of a booming building trade, families could get better homes, find employment and participate in the development of their country.
I deeply regret that the budget speech and the proposed tax reform do not contain anything in that connection. Even though in some parts of this speech, the Canadian people are led to believe that taxes have been cut, when one considers the whole speech, one realizes that the same old tax formula has been shuffled and that the Canadian taxpayer will end up paying more than before.

June 25, 1971

Even if this budget seems to bring relief to some, it is disappointing for the Canadian people.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, it is with a great deal of pleasure that I make my first intervention in the debates of this House as the member for the constituency of Brant.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
The constituency of Brant has been well described as a microcosm of Canada. It combines urban and rural areas. It uniquely reflects the critical interdependence between the industrial and agricultural sectors of our economy. It is also a riding which has suffered disastrous blows from the failures of the federal government's policies. Ottawa's war against inflation has produced a level of unemployment in Brant which is well above the national average. At the present time between
3,000	and 4,000 people are seeking employment in my constituency. At every turn their efforts to build a future based upon secure employment or to pick up the pieces after a ruinous lay-off are being hamstrung by the federal government's policies.
The strangling of Brant's economic growth because of the war against inflation has been bad enough. But Ottawa's failure to grapple with the critical issue of foreign ownership has made matters worse. Branch plant jobs in my constituency have simply been scrapped and have been exported to the United States. Student unemployment has received absolutely no federal attention at all. The hastily glued-together Opportunities for Youth program has seen fit to accept only three projects from Brant which will employ, at a maximum, only 20 students. The result is that the unemployment situation in Brant continues to be critical. Given all the economic forecasts, it is not likely to fall below 3,000 in the next 12 months and will rise sharply again this winter.
A dramatic reversal in our country's economic and agricultural policies is desperately needed if the problems of Brant and of Canada are to be solved. I would like to highlight the need for change in this country's agricultural policies. One of the major industries in Brantford is the production of farm machinery. To a considerable extent, the economic fortunes of the city are determined by how well things are going at the Massey-Ferguson plant and the White Farm Equipment plant.
When agriculture in western Canada is backed up against the wall, when wheat farmers are paid not to produce, when the federal government deliberately sets out to force people off the land and shut down farms, when prairie farmers are given stabilization payments which merely act as severance pay for their exit from the industry, when Ontario farmers face the squeeze to get out of business and receive only indifferent price support, industrial workers in my constituency are in trouble. All industrial workers suffer indirectly from a decline in agriculture, but Massey-Ferguson workers and White Farm Equipment workers are hit hard, and direct-
The Budget-Mr. Blackburn
ly, in the teeth. The federal government's task force report on agriculture does not only spell trouble for rural Canada, it spells trouble for all of Canada, and the industrial workers of my constituency are sharing the brunt of Ottawa's program to downgrade rural Canada and lower the boom on the family farm.
I wish to emphasize this point. The insecurity being generated in the agricultural sector of our economy leads directly to insecurity in much of the manufacturing sector. This troubled atmosphere is in turn reinforced by the incomprehensible economic policies of a government obsessed with the interests of bankers, oil companies, mining companies, insurance companies and, as the hon. member for Duvernay (Mr. Kierans) has pointed out, its own electoral fortunes at the expense of rational economic development.
In the name of widows and orphans the government has embarked on an anti-inflationary policy which it knew would bring misery and havoc to the lives of hundreds of thousands of Canadians. In the name of preserving our export markets it embarked on policies it knew would drive the Canadian exchange rate higher, threatening the jobs of workers in the pulp and paper industry, the petrochemical industry and, in my own constituency, a Westinghouse plant in the electronics industry. There is no consolation at all to the people of Brant in the budget proposal which removes the excise tax on television, stereo and other electronic equipment now that Westinghouse has irrevocably decided to close its plant this summer. This much needed tax relief has simply been too slow and has come too late to save this particular plant and the hundreds of jobs involved.
The government has employed its trained mandarins, particularly John Young of the Prices and Incomes Commission and Louis Rasminsky of the Bank of Canada, running around the country creating false concern about runaway inflation. There is no support for the oft expressed view of the government that inflation builds on itself. On the contrary, unemployment, especially deliberately created unemployment, leads to further stagnation, to further unemployment and to further misery. All of this is well known in Brant, particularly to the workers at Massey-Ferguson, White Farm Equipment and Stirling Action Keys Limited. When lay-offs and unemployment are the order of the day, it is apprehension and uncertainty that build on themselves. No one knows who will be next. No one knows which American-owned company will sacrifice its Canadian operation, scrap Canadian jobs and set up production elsewhere.
The Minister of Finance (Mr. Benson) cited with some satisfaction the fact that personal savings are at a record high. The minister should ask himself why this is so. In the kind of atmosphere his policies have created, a person who does not know whether he will have a job next week or next month is not going to take the little money he has left over after paying the bills to buy a new television set or a refrigerator or perhaps some little luxury that his family has been looking forward to. At a

June 25, 1971
The Budget-Mr. Blackburn
time when jobs are not secure, people save their money in case they are next to join the unemployed. You do not buy luxuries or other things you can do without for the time being when you are not even sure you will be able to pay for necessities if you are laid off. The fact that personal savings are high and that lots of consumer credit is available may seem like the best basis for an economic recovery to the minister but not to the voter, who knows that it is really a measure of the misery the minister has created.
On reading the budget presentation of the Minister of Finance I was impressed by his use of the word "confidence"-the most used and abused word in his repertoire. Everyone will agree that confidence is necessary. The Canadian people have a right to expect that their government is pursuing policies of full employment and vibrant growth. They have a right to be confident in this expectation. Unfortunately, all the minister does is talk about confidence. He does little to inspire it. Confidence is not created by saying the word over and over again. Confidence is created by clear and decisive action, not by continually asserting that up is down and black is white. Who can be confident about a government that runs away from tax reform with its tail between its legs after being bludgeoned by the American oil companies and the mining companies?
In the by-election campaign in Brant we called for tax reform. We called for the elimination of loopholes that enable big business to avoid paying their fair share of taxes. The results of the Brant by-election should have assured the minister that he need not have been afraid of the people of this country. They support tax reform. Yet what have they been given? Even the feeble half measures of the white paper on taxation, that might have been a beginning of reform, have been dropped. The corporate lobbies have been doubly successful, not only in the lavish sums of money they spent on their special interest, which is pleading "tax deductible", but they influenced the minister beyond their wildest expectations.
Low and middle-income Canadians have received a few breaks, such as the increased exemptions, the $150 deduction for working expenses, allowances for working mothers and the exemption of family homes from the capital gains tax, but the fact of the matter is that this is not tax reform. It does nothing to shift taxation on to the basis of ability to pay. It does nothing to eliminate corporate freeloading. It does nothing to close business and mining loopholes. The average Canadian will continue to pay more than his fair share of taxes. No wonder big business is smiling these days-all the way to the bank.
The economic policy section of the budget is disappointingly no more than a defence of the past policies of the government. The minister should have introduced a budget designed to achieve full employment. The people of this country want the government to demonstrate in action, not words, that it is committed to full employment. The Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) should have recognized this on his recent trip to Toronto. He was greeted by a group of workers who had been laid off at Northern Electric just last Friday. They were part of a
group of 500 workers that have been laid off in the midst of the Minister of Finance's "mythical recovery".
According to reports in the Toronto Globe and Mail and the Montreal Gazette, the Prime Minister offered jobs to the men and women who presented him with their problems, with all the aplomb of Marie Antoinette passing out cake. "I can find a job for you in Thompson", he said to one worker. "I can get a job for you in Subdbury", he said to another. If nothing else, the Prime Minister appears to have developed connections during his three years in office. If he has 4,000 more connections,
I have that many unemployed workers in my constituency who I would be happy to refer to him. One of the things he has not developed is sensitivity. To a girl who asked how he proposed she should pay her way to northern Manitoba in order to get a job, the Prime Minister replied, "Get a job as a maid." Apart from the insulting nature of his comment, surely the point is that her grievance was that she did not have a job. Advising her to solve her problem by getting a job is certainly the depth of something.
The Prime Minister also knows that Thompson, Manitoba, and Sudbury, Ontario, are not immune from lay-offs and unemployment, though I think there is probably more hope in Manitoba. Canadian workers are not lazy, as the Prime Minister would have us believe, nor do they lack initiative, as he constantly implies. They are unwilling to pack up all their belongings and leave their homes in Brantford, or Paris or elsewhere to go to Thompson and Sudbury if they are just as likely to be laid off there as they are in their own home towns. They will not trade one form of insecurity for another. The American-owned corporations of Manitoba are just as capricious as those of southern Ontario, and subject to the same pressures from abroad.
It is interesting that the Prime Minister should immediately think of Canada's resource frontier when it comes to jobs. If he would allow his thinking the freedom of moving one step further on its own, he might come to share the concern of increasing numbers of Canadians that this is precisely the area where jobs are being thrown away, or exported-largely to the United States, to be more precise.
In the long-run, structural unemployment in Canada is going to creep higher and higher unless our rich heritage of resources is processed and manufactured right here in Canada instead of being shipped abroad in their raw state giving others the jobs involved in turning them into finished products. If Canada is ever to undertake this project of using our own resources to create long-term employment for our own people, the federal government will have to get on with the job of repatriating our economy-which is even more important than the Constitution-so that we, rather than foreigners, have control over the disposition of our birthright.
In conclusion, Mr. Speaker, Canadians both urban and rural are becoming increasingly aware that the sacrifices they have been asked to make by the federal government do not make sense. They are right. They know they do not have to put up with these sacrifices, and they are not.

June 25, 1971

They are saying no to Ottawa at every available opportunity. I plead with the government, on behalf of the voters of Brant and of all Canadians, to listen to their demands for a change of direction and for full employment now, not two or three years from now.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: He needs a better speech writer than Orlikow.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker I am pleased to report about what happened in the House this week. Therefore I would like to deal with two matters that seem very important to me.
First, I shall deal with the financial statement the Minister of Finance (Mr. Benson) made last week in the House. Thus, we will be able to appreciate the efforts made by our government in order to establish a just society.
Secondly, I shall deal with the parties across the floor which are more eager to get at the government than to support its policies. So let us look together, Mr. Speaker, at the contents of this budget which the opposition has started criticizing even before reading it.
First, it has two very distinct parts: the budget itself and then the tax reform with which I shall deal.
It is suggested that the personal exemption be increased from $1,000 to $1,500, for the single citizen. Since every taxpayer will still be able to benefit from the $100 deduction, he will therefore deduct a total amount of $1,600 when he completes his income tax return. As for the individual who is married, he will be able to substract $2,950, which is quite a lot, for the time being at least.
Mr. Speaker, we have often noted that the opposition was accusing the government of neglecting senior citizens. However, the old age pension and the guaranteed income supplement were increased. Furthermore, in order to improve the situation of the aged, the government proposes that older people who are single have a personal exemption amounting to $2,250. And to those who are married, the government would eventually grant a personal exemption of $3,600.
Mr. Speaker, in order to help those families where both parents work, or the married couples of which only
The Budget-Mr. Boulanger
one partner is working, the government propose a deductible amount of $500. Such an exemption would permit a deduction for the cost of child care.
If we take a quick look at the government proposal, we find once again that the liberal party, at the federal level, is working towards an objective that has always been dear to it, that is justice and welfare for all.
Whatever some hon. members of the opposition may think, those are our views.
Mr. Speaker, the government has often been attacked with impunity, on the grounds that its policies were designed for the benefit of one class of society only, the well-to-do. It is primarily the Socialists who were constantly repeating this. Nothing is further from the truth. The provisions now brought forward attest the extent of the federal government's concern with the plight of low wage-earners. It should not be thought that the Socialists alone are anxious to protect the small wage-earner: we constantly have him in mind, whatever the opposition may say to the contrary. When I say "the opposition", I am excluding the official opposition which seems, to my view, somewhat less fanatical than some Socialists and Creditistes, although they nevertheless are the opposition.
But the Socialists, with their twaddle, deserve to be told our way of thinking from time to time and that is what I am trying to do. In my view there are different classes in the opposition, when you compare the Conservation opposition and smaller parties, such as Socialists and Creditistes.
There are differences in class between members of the House, among whom there are specialists, experts and men of responsibility.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Some time ago, Mr. Speaker, the government hastened to elaborate policies for the purpose of creating jobs-

Regardless of whether you believe it ot not.

The budget presented before this House on December 3, 1970, contained a series of measures and programs designed to stimulate the economy both on a short- and a long-term basis. They were all aimed, Mr. Speaker, at improving the conditions of those who are entitled to benefit from this society of plenty, like anyone else.
When we hear socialists claiming to be able to solve our country's problem with a single stroke of a pencil or by coming to power, as they have been dreaming of
June 25, 1971

The Budget-Mr. Boulanger
doing it for a long time, it becomes apparent that they are not always telling the truth.
This budget then should be considered as an expansionary budget which gives satisfaction to all Canadians, since it involves a reduction in the tax burden. Thanks to this budget, we will be in a better position to help increase the taxpayer's purchasing power and hence to promote our economic growth.
In this budget, Mr. Speaker, the government suggests a change of definition for income, so that our fiscal policy be more equitable to the taxpayer in general. We suggest that more so far untaped elements of income be included in the definition, including deduction of new expenses from taxable income.
Taking a close look at those proposals, Mr. Speaker, we observe that the reform of the tax system applies mostly to salary and wage earners who constitute the greatest number of taxpayers. It is then only reasonable that the salaried man should have a word to say in this matter. This is not the view of the socialists alone; we think so too.
The federal government, as always, aims at easing the burden of low income people.
In the same line of reasoning, he insists that small businesses should also take advantage of their Canadian "citizenship". In fact, the government of Ottawa is of the opinion that the tax system should support the ventures of free enterprise.
Let us remember that the Canadian economy depends on the vitality and aggressiveness of small but developing concerns. The reduced rate of taxation now applicable to part of their income is insufficient as an incentive. However, the proposed adjustment of this rate can be useful in encouraging initiative by helping small companies to accumulate enough capital for their expansion.
In conclusion, I would like to say that this tax system seems more effective and more equitable. As the Minister of Finance once said, if we start from the principle that our society is undergoing a deep change, we cannot but agree that the tax reform answers the changing needs. Mr. Speaker, the very foundation of our society lies on private enterprise, whatever the socialists may say. Those whom we call the small wage earners must be made to benefit from the principle of justice in Canada. This is why I think the budget brought down by the Minister of Finance is the result of a sustained effort to strike a balance between justice and free enterprise.
As for the oppositon, I think it is less a real opposition to the proposed measures than a traditional negative criticism lacking any sense of co-operation. I sincerely think the government could introduce any kind of measure and the opposition would immediately start crying blue murder without even asking themselves if it is needed legislation. This is why I have no intention of prosecuting the opposition for I would only be playing their own game.
When I talk of the opposition, I mean particularly the little opposition-the socialists and the Creditistes. I shall
restrict myself to quoting figures and examples showing that the opposition parties quite often direct more or less serious criticisms at the government and, often, at the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau). That will be the conclusion of my comments.
It is unfortunate that the member for Abitibi (Mr. Laprise) left the House. There is one Creditiste member remaining, who is a good friend, and I hope he can accept my remarks. The famous official leader of the Social Credit, the member for Temiscamingue (Mr. Caouette), seems to possess the necessary qualifications to be a politician and to be devoted to his work in the House, which he never leaves. By his own account, he is always here to accomplish a never-ending task. I am going to give you some information that may surprise many, Mr. Speaker, including the Creditistes on the other side. For the past few months, opposition parties, particularly-and I mean "particularly"-the Ralliement Creditiste, which we now call Credit social in French and Social Credit in English, to avoid confusion with the party of the Premier of British Columbia, have tried to create the impression that the Prime Minister is not in Ottawa often enough and that he travels too much.
I hope hon. members are paying special attention to my remarks. I conducted a little survey of my own, as assistant government whip, and I found in Hansard the following statistics: out of 250 votes taken in the House from the 1968 election to June 1971, the Rt. Hon. Prime Minister, member for Mount Royal, participated in 190, which represents an average attendance in the House of 76 per cent. The Leader of the official Opposition, the hon. member for Halifax, (Mr. Stanfield), participated in 183 votes, or an average of 70.3 per cent, and the new socialist leader, the hon. member for York South (Mr. Lewis) participated in 170 votes, for a 68 per cent average. As far as the miracle worker is concerned, the leader of the Ralliement Creditiste, he took part in 44 votes out of 250 that is an average attendance in the House of 17.6 per cent. Those are the exact figures, and no nonsense. The famous leader of the Ralliement Creditiste always throws to our faces: You are never in attendance in the House, you, government members! This is an example of his famour work in the House.
For a member who continually talks about the banking system and who, as a member of the Committee on Finance, Trade and Economic Affairs, has studied the banking system reform and is supposed to be an expert in the matter, he attended none of the committee meetings during the previous Parliament. This means that the Social Credit leader is no more thoughtful in the House than he is elsewhere. It is high time we stopped taking him seriously.
Here is a further example of statements by another member of the Creditiste opposition. Hardly a few days after the election in Trois-Rivieres-I was waiting for a special opportunity to reply and I am taking advantage of the debate on the budget statement to do so-the hon. member for Shefford (Mr. Rondeau), whom I call the whip-socket and the train-bearer of the Social Credit leader-took the floor to express another platitude. He
[Mr. Boulanger.)
June 25, 1971

started a silly rumour to stir some members or provoke laughter because he finds his platitudes so funny that he laughs about them as he tells them. It was on my return from the by-election in Trois-Rivieres where I had the honour to work for our candidate, now member for Trois-Rivieres (Mr. Lajoie), who has won, in my opinion, a well deserved victory. The hon. member for Shefford rose in one of these early morning moods, not quite awake, yet bright enough to think of telling this House a good joke. He asked the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development (Mr. Chretien): Is the hon. member for Mercier going to have the hot pants that he promised delivered to the ladies in Trois-Rivieres?
Let me say that the ladies are truly pretty in Trois-Rivieres. I did see some of them in hot pants, and they were a sight for sore yes. But, unfortunately, I never thought of making such a deal. So, this is a lie, a falsehood and a platitude such as the hon. member is capable of.
I know that the platitude he said is a lie, because I never at any time pronounced a public speech, first of all because there was no meeting. We had society meetings, and we made door to door calls, but never such platitudes as those were uttered by me or our new House member. However, I can say to the hon. member for Shefford that if I ever have to offer hot pants, I would offer him a pair which would fit a three year old child, because I suppose his intellectual quotient is about the same as a child's that age.
Here is the way some of those so-called defenders of the Canadian race, experts in everything, behave-in English we would say: Jack of all trades, master of none. I took this opportunity to answer them. It is not in my nature to make personal remarks, but I have been attacked falsely, first by the leader of the Social Credit, who accuses me of never being present in this House. In fact, I have always been here, except last year when I had a car accident. If I answered back, it was to make him and the member for Shefford understand that platitudes or lies should not be made publicly.
In conclusion, I will try to be a little nicer and point out that some members should at least in the House be more serious than they have been for some time. I agree that opposition is necessary in the House, but we should not witness the things to which I referred.
I hope that the members opposite, especially the Socialists, will refrain from playing politics, that they will try to be a little more serious and stop discrediting other members. Whether we are Socialists, Creditistes, Conservatives or Liberals I know that we are here to help the Canadian people and not to say platitudes we hear all day long. By criticizing the government in this way we contribute to depreciate the House of Commons and the representatives of the people. I hope that my advice will be followed once and for all.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the budget as it pertains to what is left of 1971 is virtually of no consequence. The consen-
The Budget-Mr. Peddle
sus of almost every expert in the country who has looked at this budget and the very modest measures embodied in it is that it will have virtually no effect upon the desperate employment situation we now have in the province of Newfoundland.
To begin with, the removal of the 3 per cent surtax would mean for the vast majority of the wage and salary earners in that province a tax reduction that would barely equal the cost of a bottle of Newfoundland screech. Since it is 3 per cent for only a half year and not for a full year, I doubt very much, if a half bottle were obtainable, that it would buy a half bottle of screech; but since many people in Newfoundland cannot afford it now because one-fifth of them are on welfare, it means virtually nothing.
It is obvious that the Minister of Finance (Mr. Benson) should have cut taxes last December. Instead, he chose to greatly expand government spending, which is typical of the Liberal approach to things, that the government knows better how to spend the people's money than the people do themselves. In my province, whenever we have any money we do not need anybody to tell us how to spend it. The trouble is that the Minister of Finance has kept the tax rate so high that he has not left anything to spend anyway, even if the people of Newfoundland had any jobs.
As for the so-called tax reform, in Newfoundland we have an expression for a big noise that does not mean anything, that is, a great big thunderstorm with very little rain. It is fair to say that the minister's tax changes for next year are a lot better than those proposed in the white paper but, as someone has said, it is somewhat like the relief one feels when one thinks he has cancer in both lungs and the doctor tells him it is only in one.
What started out as a catastrophe in the white paper finally wound up as just more of the finance minister's patching and painting of the same leaky, old hull. He can keep fixing, stitching, patching and scratching until Moby Dick comes in again, but the old ship ain't going to float any better. I could compare this government to the old vessel, the Avalon Voyageur, that plied the route between the island part of Newfoundland and Labrador last summer. Much needed to be done to her; she was in bad shape. The Department of Transport insisted that so many alterations needed to be done that the owners decided there was only one sensible thing to do and that was to scrap her. I am suggesting that the only thing the people of Canada can do today to this leaky old government is scrap it.

All these changes, these so-called tax reforms, are hardly worth, as we say down our way, a bucket of caplin at the height of the season. The minister could easily have done this three years ago. given relief to such people as old age pensioners who are receiving a guaranteed income supplement, and those in the very low-income bracket. subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: It is good for the paper industry.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I am sure it was not devised for that. What I am suggesting is that as we go on, the budget gets heavier and heavier. It is the typical Liberal outlook. When times get tough and the obvious explanations will not suffice, you offer a little more and a little faster, you put in a few more inches and pounds of paper and the poor, unsuspecting public will think it is a great thing.
Today we celebrate, for want of a better word-"celebrate" is not the word I would like to use, but the right word escapes me-the third year of the emperor's reign. In 1968 he convinced the multitudes that following June 25 of that year their society would become pervaded by sweetness and light and, above all, by justice. He convinced them, also, that their various regions, by the simple expedient of a fair distribution of the nation's great wealth, would be cleansed forever of that pestilential curse known as regional disparity. So the multitudes, with some exceptions from the far east and from the far west, flocked to the polls to register their approval of this saviour who had so skillfully appeared to promise nothing while promising everything.
I will not quote his exact words but will paraphrase what he said. He said, "I will not be browbeaten and intimidated into making promises. Other, lesser politicians have been guilty of that and I despise that type of dishonest approach to the electorate." What he said in effect was, "I will simply promise a just society and the unceasing efforts of my government toward the elimination of regional disparity." So three years ago today the electorate pondered this and came to the conclusion that no one in Canada could possibly wish for anything more than complete justice and equality.
The Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) promised the moon, at the same time deploring the lesser politicians who had made promises of more industries, highways, social security, employment and such mundane things. We know the results. Following June 25, 1968, the multitudes waited with bated breath for the society to become more just and for regional disparity to disappear. Some expected that some of the things would come to pass on the morning of June 26, but alas, three years have passed and what do we find? We find that unemployment, which for a number of years was a really serious problem only in certain pockets or areas of the country, has become a desperate problem all across the country. We could say, in a negative sense I suppose, that regional disparity has been decreased in that now the unemployed in Newfoundland can take great consolation from the fact that thousands now are unemployed in British Columbia, Ontario, Quebec, and so on. That is very small consolation.
We know what happened to the just society. The Prime Minister himself would now rather avoid that expression. He admits it was only a slogan, and right now he does not believe too much in slogans. But it was a pretty serious business about the month of June, 1968. It was not labelled then as only a slogan. I have not given any particular thought to this question but it might be a good time now to deal with in a cursory way the accomplishments of the government which is three years old today.
One of the things that stands out is the emasculation of Parliament, the spreading of Parliament all over this area known as Parliament Hill-all the different offices, and so on. It is part of the system of checks and balances. As part of that system the Prime Minister introduced participatory democracy. The Prime Minister considerably legalized abortions, and as a part of his checks and balances system he recognized the Vatican, and later on arranged for family allowances to be increased. He recognized Red China, visited Russia and signed a protocol, whatever that is. He completely ignores the United States, or does almost the next thing to it.
He recognized the status of women. He gave some recognition to it anyway, and shortly afterwards he married. If anybody asks him now, he says, "The wife is home working, washing the dishes"-just what a good wife should be doing. He deliberately increased unemployment-that is a fact by his own admission-and to balance that we have an increase in unemployment insurance coming up. One could go all the way down the list and find this system of checks and balances; that is the only way I know how to describe it. Somebody said that this budget was a cosmetic job. Well, it is quite a mud-pack; but I say that on close scrutiny, which it is receiving now from the Canadian people, it will be found that many wrinkles have not been covered. The hon. member who preceded me dwelt a good bit on hot pants. I do not know what that has to do with it.
We had a great furore the night the so-called budget, the tax reform documents were delivered. Hon. gentlemen who backed the Minister of Finance figured "This is it." Had an election been called that night it might very well have been it because the people of Canada might not have been given an opportunity to give any kind of analysis to this five pounds of political pap.
The budget mentions margarine. I do not want to play on words but I cannot help but feel it is a budget with something for everyone and very little for anyone. The word "margarine" conjures up the idea of something to spread and it is my honest opinion that this budget, while it offers something for everybody it is spread pretty darned thin and by the time next year comes around there will be many people having second thoughts. So despite his protestations to the contrary, I think it might be a good idea if the Prime Minister did

June 25, 1971

call an election this fall before people really start to analyse this budget and see it for what it is worth.
While it is not an election budget, as some people have said, I think that it could be. The Prime Minister, his cohorts, helpers, and what have you, are going all across the country now. He has started to try to gauge the reaction of the people to this budget. Recently we watched the Prime Minister. As I say, he is travelling the country trying to repeat the magic of 1968. I have been watching television. I do not think it is my party prejudice that is responsible, but I notice a difference in the ages of the people gathering around the Prime Minister when he goes into school areas and shopping plazas. I will admit that there are still squeals, but I suggest they are halfhearted. I suggest they have a hollow ring to them.
Most hon. members will remember when they stopped believing in Santa Claus but did not feel quite ready to let their parents in on that fact. They did not want their parents to feel bad. Their parents were enjoying the idea of Santa Claus, so the children said, "We will let them go on believing that we believe in Santa Claus for another year." This is how I figure out the type of squeals that are now coming.

These are the people who are attached to the Prime Minister's office and who are in other departments of government psychoanalysing people. The government, in my humble opinion, has done everything in the last three years but govern responsibly.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I would have the hon. member who just interjected know that I am one of those who is putting up some of the fancy scotch on the fact that the Prime Minister would not dare call an election this fall.
This is a government of sweeping reforms, omnibus bills, deliberate confusion almost too bold to comprehend. The idea is: We will do what we want. The people of Canada expected more and in 1968 they were led to believe they would get more. They did not expect the Prime Minister to follow the old line of politics that has been going on since time immemorial-three or four years of doing what they like and then a buttered-up budget that says: Though we have done everything we could to hurt you in the last three years, now we have given you relief in taxes and you will give us another mandate so that we can do it all again.
The people of this country expected more, Mr. Speaker, and I expected more. For some time I had a little admiration for the Prime Minister because he gave the impression he was going to give the Canadian people something different. However, he has turned out to be one of the same old gang, only worse. If it is unfair to tax that supple-

If it is unfair now to give some tax relief to the low-income people, surely it has been unfair for a number of years. Why must they wait 5i years? There is no reason in the world, Mr. Speaker, except the one that I have mentioned: If you want ice cream you have to take your cod liver oil. What about the $500 extra exemption? What about the people who paid tax on that all those years: are they now supposed to automatically support this government? Absolute nonsense!
The results of the seven provincial elections in the last year or so show that people are not going to start thanking the government for a measure introduced just before an election. They are going to develop memories and kick out any government trying to play that kind of game. If a business corporation engaged in such deliberate confusion, such blatant deception, such misrepresentation such blindfolding of the devil in the dark, the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs (Mr. Basford) would move in and have the principals in jail before you could say Jack Robinson.
In my opinion, the only way this government could be re-elected is if all the voters in Canada went on pot on polling day and voted in a rosy, love-everybody stupor. They could not be expected to return this government from any practical, common sense considerations.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I wish to commend the hon. member for Grand Falls-White Bay-Labrador (Mr. Peddle) for his enthusiasm in reminding hon. members of this House of the great event that took place three years ago today, the election of the party I represent.
