subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is an honour and a privilege for me to take part in this debate on the budget brought down on Friday, June 18th, by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Benson). This document was anxiously awaited by all Canadians because it follows the White Paper which was an important step in the evolution of the Canadian democracy.
The White Paper was tabled almost 18 months ago. Its object was to propose the required tax reforms through which the prosperity of the whole population could be ensured. The White Paper was the result of a popular consultation which gave rise to many comments, and even criticisms, some useful, constructive as well as considered suggestions likely to help the government in elaborating a tax policy for and by Canadians. It must be repeated here, for some may have already forgotten, that the White Paper was only a popular consultation, and not a draft bill changing the tax policy.
The new budget will ensure a better distribution of the tax burden Canadians must accept in order to keep
enjoying all the services provided by the federal government.
Mr. Speaker, I hope that my contribution to this debate will influence those who were unfavourably impressed.
During the entire speech of the Minister of Finance, the faces of opposition members, who seemed to undergo a Chinese torture, expressed very well the feelings that came over them as the tax measures in the budget were announced, and what the opposition considered a hardship was greeted by all Canadians with enthusiasm and relief.
One needs only to read editorials and see the general public's reaction to realize that the popular and realistic budget measures will bring prosperity to Canada, but that will not prevent the people opposite, who seem to lack of imagination, to reel off their aggressive nonsense.
The Canadian people already look upon them without sympathy. They are greatly disappointed by the favorable response expressed by the Canadian people.

Let us examine some of the measures, particularly those that are going to benefit the average worker, that is, the majority of the taxpayers; the measures which will bring to every working Canadian a larger share of the wealth of the nation.

of heavy fuels and which represents for the pulp and paper industry a saving of over $3,500,000.
The reduction of the taxes applying to petrochemical raw materials will also assist this industry. The petrochemical industry has deserved the support and admiration of Parliament; it is among those which have made the greatest technological progress in Canada. It is therefore important that this industry should keep on making progress and remain in the forefront of modern industries.
It is a disgrace that the leader of the opposition (Mr. Stanfield) should refuse to realize the numerous possibilities offered by the budget to fight unemployment. Well before the budget debate is over and even before we can benefit from all the budgetary measures, I am sure we will be blamed for pump-priming economy, for creating new employment and for restoring consumers' confidence just to create inflation.
The budget contains several measures which will gradually deal with our unacceptable and unfair unemployment situation to the benefit of the many citizens who want to contribute to their country's prosperity.

In their speeches, opposition members keep on forecasting that unemployment rate will sustain no decrease. Their speeches are a tissue of lies. One might wonder whether they want unemployment to increase rather than decrease.
The Quebec government has already expressed satisfaction about the federal government's recommendations concerning the tax reforms put forward in the budget, saying that the federal government has taken into account the recommendations made throughout the consultations. Such a statement is a faithful interpretation of the feelings of most Canadians in my province, which was confirmed when I had an opportunity to approach a large number of my fellow citizens on the matter since the introduction of the budget.

The 4,700,000 taxpayers, Mr. Speaker, who will see a reduction of their share of taxes do not agree with the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Stanfield) who claimed on television that the budget is a washout. The one million taxpayers who would have paid taxes next year but who have been removed from the tax rolls because of greater exemptions do not share the opinion of the opposition parties when they call the budget a flop.
All taxpayers who claim married status and derive their income solely through wages and salaries will pay less taxes in 1972 than they are now paying. Also, all those filing as single taxpayers and making $8,000 a year or less as income from their employment will be paying less tax. The measures that favour working mothers will have the effect of making it easier for them to rejoin and remain in the labour force if they wish. That is a widespread practice of the seventies which brings in first-class labour. All the measures enumerated in the budget will mean improvements in personal disposal income,
The Budget-Mr. Dupras
thus creating a greater demand for goods and services and, undoubtedly, an increase in personal savings.
Many people will not agree with those who resist progress for the sake of being against the government and, for the sake of gaining political popularity, resist any evolution in the administration of this great country of ours. The opposition is saying that the Liberals only look at figures and graphs and not at people, yet in the same breath they call this an election budget. They should make up their minds; they cannot have it both ways. As they have said, you can't have the best of two worlds. Perhaps we should accept the fact that a party which has been away from power as long it has tend to develop a negative approach to everything that is progressive, and becomes deplorably hopeless.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: How true.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Of course, the parties that never have exercised power, and never will, can promise almost anything and continue to live in a make-believe world. This budget has permitted Canadians to rediscover the acrobatic talents of the Leader of the Official Opposition and other opposition parties which have admitted in public their approval of a good number of the budgetary measures. The Leader of the Opposition even ventured to say that the budget contains many good features. Of course it does. The people of Canada know it and the media know it, as do all of us here; however, not all will admit it.
Now, Mr. Speaker, I would like to deal with another subject, which has to do with the answer given by the Premier of the province of Quebec on the proposed charter of Victoria. The leader of the New Democratic Party should be reminded that he is not authorized to speak on behalf of the population of the province of Quebec.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE

speechtext:
That is no wonder when we consider who leads that party in Quebec, Mr. Speaker. The intervention of the leader of that party today was in very bad taste and I deny him the right to speak for a population that has so strongly rejected his party.

Mr. Speaker, before concluding, I would like to make some sense-if possible-out of the statement made by the hon. member for Prince Edward-Hastings (Mr. Hees), which has bewildered the members of his party, as usual. Recognizing the great popularity of this budget, he forecasts general elections in the fall.
May I be allowed to take advantage of his great generosity and have my name put on his long list of future beneficiaries?

June 25, 1971
The Budget-Mr. Thompson
Other statements from other members of his party, and as bewildering, remind me of Chantecler, the rooster which held that his vocal morning performances caused the sun to rise.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in the few minutes left at my disposal this afternoon I want to make a few pertinent comments about the budget. I must say that this budget is a lawyer's and accountant's dream, because its full impact and all its intricacies and complications will not be known to taxpayers until accountants, lawyers, Members of Parliament and officials of the Department of Finance have become more familiar with the many proposals that the budget presents.
There are a few points on the positive side for which I should like to give credit. The raising of the personal allowances to $1,500 and $2,850 is long overdue and is a good step forward. After all, it is 22 years since the former tax allowance of $1,000 was established, and the cost of living has more than doubled since then. The increase in the level of deductions applicable to senior citizens and the lowering of the qualifying age to 65 are also good moves. However, they are of little benefit to those who are not subject to income tax; they do not help those in the low-income bracket who pay no tax anyway.
I believe, also, that the dropping of the 3 per cent surtax is a positive step. I only wish there had been a measure of relief extended to those who are in greatest need as far as the working poor are concerned. I have in mind the four million or five million people whose earnings barely enable them to cope with the increased cost of living. There is not a member of this House who is not aware that many of his constituents are working for wages of between $60 and $100 a week. They have jobs, they are working, but they are nevertheless living in a measure of poverty.
I should like to compliment the minister on having doubled the deductible allowance in connection with charitable giving-the percentage has been raised from 10 per cent to 20 per cent. This is an incentive measure which helps the private sector to support many worthwhile organizations whose efforts obviously contribute to society and even save the government money. Even at the proposed new level I note we are still behind the United States, where the rate is 30 per cent, but the 20 per cent rate will be of great help to a large number of people and to church organizations and it represents a good step forward.
I think it is logical that organized sport should be included in the category qualifying as the recipients of charitable giving. This is a way of helping organized sport and athletics without increasing government handouts to a greater extent than at the present time. At the appropriate time I intend to move an amendment to include gifts given for international development or aid in this category of charitable giving. A new organization has been set up with CIDA; it is now called the non-government organizational department. I believe the money which the government spent last year and during the present year in sharing international development and relief costs with the private sector has resulted in better value being obtained than would otherwise have been the case. 1 do not think there is a better way of encouraging the private sector to share in the cost of international development or emergency aid than by allowing it the same kind of incentive as far as the tax deduction permitted for charitable giving is concerned.
There seems to be in the budget another important aspect, the fact that 750,000 people have been struck off the tax rolls. That appears a great step forward on the surface, but really the amount of money collected in the past from this group of taxpayers at the bottom of the tax rolls has barely been sufficient to defray the cost of collection. Thus, the Minister of Finance (Mr. Benson) has taken a step which is, after all, only logical. The removal of the estate tax is also, seemingly, a wise step to take especially bearing in mind the debates we have had in the House concerning this tax.
However, when one considers that the capital gains tax will produce more for the government from estates than the estate tax ever did, removal of the latter tax is not the positive step forward it appears to be on the surface. Then again, in my home province, as is the case in Saskatchewan, the provincial share, the 75 per cent of this tax collected, is refunded to the estate itself. Unless provision is made within the forthcoming legislation to allow for these circumstances, Parliament will be discriminating against the people who live in these two provinces and are entitled to this deduction according to provincial law.
With regard to the gift tax, it would seem good that it has been eliminated but as far as I can understand from the budget, so has the whole question of gifts. Thus, as the government takes away the gift tax it also takes away the allowances which might have been deductible for gifts under the old system and it really is of no advantage whatsoever. In fact, the opposite is the case.
I cannot help being concerned about the situation as it relates to the farmer. I know the basic herd concept will be allowed to continue until the end of the year. After that the capital gains arrangement will take over. It seems to me a type of legislation which has had good effect and which has been helpful to farmers in the past will be neutralized by the livestock farmer having to pay more taxes.
Another aspect I wish to mention concerns the arrangements for straight line depreciation. While it is true it will apply to assets acquired before the new system starts, depreciation will be calculated on a diminishing balance system with respect to assets acquired after the new arrangement has come into effect. In the recapture of appreciation, capital gains proposals will apply, so when he purchases equipment a farmer will find he is subject to capital gains tax on the recaptured depreciation.
Mr. Speaker, I see it is five o'clock. As we are nearing the end of the day, might I ask for five minutes more in

June 25, 1971

which to finish my remarks so that we shall be free to begin with a new speaker on Monday?

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Is the House agreeable to allowing the hon. member to continue for five minutes?

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Agreed.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I shall not take time in which to illustrate this contention, but in the buying of a farm tractor and allowing the permissible depreciation to be taken off each year, when the tractor has finished its usefulness and is turned in for another tractor the recaptured value will be subject to capital gains tax. As far as I can see, in the example I have given it would cost a farmer as much as $500, $700 or even $1,000 in capital gains tax representing tax he has not paid before.
Under present-day estate tax arrangements all farm land valued at less than $100,000 is free of estate tax. However, under the capital gains tax proposal, if the land increases in value after valuation day the farmer will be called upon to pay a capital gains tax of 50 per cent at his going rate of tax at that time. So I do not think this legislation is likely to improve the position of the farmer. In fact, as far as I can see this budget will continue to work hardship by increasing the amount of tax taken from farmers who are in a difficult enough situation whether in the Maritimes, central Canada or the west. I am most concerned in this regard.
In the over-all picture of the budget I should like to say that while we can give credit for the reduction of certain types of taxes, the general "take" of the government, on the other hand, will be much more than it was before. Obviously, you cannot take more and at the same time expect to lower the over-all amount of taxes, as the government tries to give the impression. In this regard, moving into the capital gains area, I find that the budget is certainly not as basically sound in the matter of what is called tax reform as it ought to be. I do not believe that a capital gains tax is a type of tax that we should have had at this time in Canada.
In an industrialized economy I believe it is a fair tax, but we are a long way from being industrialized. Tremendous resource development must take place if our economy is to be viable. This is why I do not think the time has come when we can enjoy the luxury of this type of tax. But if it had to come, it seems to me that the government would have been far better advised to have given a lower rate of tax recognition to long-term investment as compared to quick profit, speculative gain.
We want to encourage the Canadian people to invest their savings in the development of this country. We already have one of the highest rate of savings of any developed country in the world. It seems to me there should be a greater direct participation on the part of Canadian citizens in investment in industry and resource development in Canada. Therefore, if there had to be a
The Budget-Mr. Thompson
capital gains tax it seems to me the government would have been well advised to assess capital gains earned from long-term investment at a much lower rate than the rate applied to speculative gains and quick turnovers. I think a distinction should have been made.
I am also concerned that the budget will not give the incentive to the economy of this country that it should have given. The statistics we have received for the month of May show a greater number of Canadians working than in April, with a somewhat comparative decrease in the number of unemployed, giving the picture that we are solving unemployment, and I do not think this is the case. At the present time, the seasonally adjusted rate of unemployment is 6.3 per cent, way above the average figure of 4 per cent that the Minister of Finance said was acceptable in this country. There ought to have been ways devised whereby there would be a greater incentive to the economy of the country than that given by this budget. In fact, even the parts of the budget for which I commend the government are not going to give any genuine incentive to the economy as a whole.
I could go on to discuss other aspects of the budget, but time today does not really permit me to do so. However, in closing I do want to mention the situation relating to the over-all budgetary position of the government in the fiscal year 1970-71. As far as the estimates contained in the budget papers before us are concerned, we find the Minister of Finance budgeting for a $417.6 million deficit. If this forecast deficit is like the previous budgetary forecasts of the Minister of Finance, it will prove to be much more than this figure. He had expected a surplus of $300 million. This kind of deficit spending, for the return that we can expect from the budget, seems to me to be entirely out of reason.
Thus, although to fully understand and to see the effects of the budget will require time, I do not believe the picture is nearly as rosy and optimistic as the Minister of Finance has said it is. However, as I have said, compared with the white paper the budget is a good one. Certainly the retraction of a number of tax reform policies outlined in the white paper has given a greater sense of encouragement to Canadians across the scene. On the other hand, compared with the present system of taxation it is my opinion that this budget does not really represent any basic tax reform. We are still trying to shore-up the old approach toward equitable taxation, and it is a tragedy that the budget really did not get down to the genuine tax reform that our taxation system requires.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR PAYMENTS TO RETIRED CITIZENS AND OTHERS TO ASSIST HANDICAPPED CHILDREN
speechtext: Explain.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR PAYMENTS TO RETIRED CITIZENS AND OTHERS TO ASSIST HANDICAPPED CHILDREN
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, the purpose of this bill is to help provide, at small cost, the touch of compassion which, of necessity, cannot be legislated into our statutes that provide expert care and custodial treatment, at great cost, to those of our children who are dispossessed of the kingdom that should be theirs: the handicapped in mind, body or spirit, the deserted, the neglected or the parentless. The bill proposes to establish a fund out of which expenses for transportation, meals and the like would be paid to retired citizens who could thus spend some of their time and share some of their love with children who are robbed or bereft of their birthright. The emotional and psychological enrichment to both age levels is obvious.

DEPARTMENT OF SUPPLY AND SERVICES-MAN-HOURS SAVED AS A RESULT OF USE OF COMPUTERS
speechtext: How many man-hours have been saved as a result of the utilization of computers by the Department of Supply and Services and Receiver General of Canada during each year since computers have been used?

speakeroldname: Hon. James Richardson (Minister of Supply and Services):
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF SUPPLY AND SERVICES-MAN-HOURS SAVED AS A RESULT OF USE OF COMPUTERS
speechtext:
The Department of Supply and Services became a Department on April 1, 1969 as a result of the Government Organization Act (1969). The new Department is composed of the former Department of Defence Production, the Comptroller of the Treasury, Department of Public Printing and Stationery, the Bureau of Management Consulting Services and the Central Data Processing Bureau.
Records of man-hour utilization were not kept by these various components in sufficient detail to enable this question to be answered.
However, the following statistics of the office of the Comptroller of the Treasury from the time of the first use of computers in 1961 until 1967 may be helpful in determining the workload volumes of major computer applications. For example, the personnel strength of the Comptroller of the Treasury in 1961 was 4,467 and this staff was increased in six years by only 47 persons to bring the total to 4,514 personnel. The workload growth for the number of cheques issued and reconciled annually increased from 53,000,000 in 1961 to 87,697,000 in 1967; the number of transactions processed into accounting statements was 2,520,000 for 1962 and rose to 10,176,000 by 1967.
As a result of the Government announcement in July, 1968 and the coming into force on April 1, 1969, of the Government Organization Act (1969) the Comptroller of the Treasury, the Central Data Processing Bureau and the Bureau of Management Consulting Services formed the Services Administration of the new Department of Supply and Services. Accordingly, it is not possible now to relate the workload statistics by computers to the utilization of man-hours of this new component of the Department of Supply and Services to the above statistics.
In the other areas of the Department, namely, the Data Processing Branch of the Printing Bureau of the Supply Administration, together with the Computer Services Bureau, the Data Processing Bureau and the Management Consulting Branch of the Services Administration, com-
Questions
puters have been and are being used for a variety of functions, many of which would probably not have been undertaken had the computers not been available.

speechtext: I am informed that the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation is conscious that it should reflect the life and interests of senior citizens. No specific program series exists or is being planned, but the CBC is aware that it has a social responsibility in ensuring that elderly people do not lose their sense of participation in Canadian society. It is felt that the national broadcasting service of the CBC provides a balanced program fare of information, enlightenment and entertainment to meet the widely varying tastes of all ages, classes, geographical and other groups, in reasonably fair proportion. Some of the program series which have featured material of special interest to elderly people include "Voice of the Pioneer", "Matinee", "Concern", "Gerussi", "A votre service", "Un homme vous ecoute", and "Present", on radio, and "Take 30", 'Tuesday Night", "Weekend", "Man Alive", "Format 30", "Format 60" and "Femme d'aujourd'hui", on television. CBC production personnel have been asked to keep in mind the contribution that can be made to national broadcasting by elderly persons because of their past experience and knowledge.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have listened, like all the other hon. members the budget speech delivered last week by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Benson), some called it a pre-election speech, that will not change much to the present situation.
Mr. Speaker, I believe the second point is nearer the truth. By the way, if we look at what happened in Saskatchewan last week, just a few days after the famous budget, the Liberals were given a warning by losing the elections in that province. Had the voters of that province been interested in the budget, I think that the Liberals would have stayed in power.
The same situation prevails now, not only in Saskatchewan, but almost everywhere in this country. I say that the budget of the Minister of Finance will not create a single job in Canada, will not generate any new industry and will perhaps prove unable to keep the present industries in operation.
Mr. Speaker, this is an obvious budget, a red herring across the trail of the electorate. It mentions, for instance, that the basic non taxable amount for single persons will be $1,500 instead of $1,000 and $2,850 instead of $2,000 for married people. We have been asking for some at least ten years exemptions of $3,000 for single people and $5,000 for married people because we know that if wage earners keep their salaries for their expenses, when they buy products they are subject to an indirect federal tax. And yet the government gets a large share of the money spent by Canadian taxpayers and consumers. This is why we find the exemptions suggested in the budget clearly inadequate. In fact, a saving of $25 or $30 a year does not increase considerably the income, the purchasing power of the consumer.
Now, with exemptions up to $1,500 and $2,850 being granted, the budget makes unemployment benefits and scholarships subject to taxation, which was not the case formerly. Finally, this year's budget is one and a half billion dollars higher than last year's and this billion and a half the government is getting from the pockets of Canadian taxpayers. Even if the government says "We have relieved a million Canadians from taxation", if it must overtax five or six million people in order to balance the budget supplement of a billion and a half dollars, Canadians on the whole will be no better off. There could only be one justification for taxes, and that would be full employment, as a result of which production would be inadequate to meet the requirements of the whole population because of high consumption on the part of some of the population.
But this is not the case today. In fact, the history of taxation as an expedient is based on two propositions: first, that the poor would become richer by making the rich poorer; second, that it is a justifiable procedure to support a system of accumulation of wealth while arbitrarily confiscating part of this wealth. The latter proposition is like saying that the object or purpose of a 24171-47
The Budget-Mr. Caouette
hockey team is to score goals but that if more than a
certain number are scored, any number in excess will not count.
Let us first consider the first assertion to the effect that the poor are poor, that the less poor are less poor and that the poor would become richer. That is the line of reasoning of the right hon. Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau), of the government and of the present system. This assertion arises from the confusion that exists between money and real wealth.
It is alleged, in the first place, that there is absolute equality. Economists say so. There is complete equality between actual wealth and money, and therefore the standard of living of the community would be enhanced if anyone having much money as compared to his neighbour was taxed, even though the amount of said taxation was not fully passed on to the less fortunate neighbour, which is more often than not the case.
That this argument is absurd is self evident if it is applied, for instance, to those who own a Cadillac. Should every owner of such a car be taxed according to his standard of living, it does not follow in the least that those people who do not own a car or who own a Volkswagen would be able to buy Cadillacs.
This simply means that fewer Cadillacs would be produced. It would certainly be a good thing if the production scheme could transfer the Cadillac employees elsewhere and have them produce real and desirable resources.
We realize that this is excatly what happens in times of war when production of luxury items stops. But in time of war we do not have unemployment or this surplus of unsold production. However, under the present financial system stopping the sale of Cadillacs would mean higher unemployment, and full employment is the best way of keeping people in slavery.
All those arguments arise from the suggestion that production of real resources, that is those money can buy, is completely separate from production of the money allowing people to buy them and that by taxing all but bankers we increase the monopolizing power of the money makers.
Fortunately, it is not necessary today to develop extensively this argument since it has ceased to be discussed in financial and economical circles. In Volume 15 of the Encyclopaedia Britannica we read:
Banks make loans by creating credit. They create means of payment out of nothing.
Or again according to the president of the Midland Bank: "The monetary mass in circulation varies through the action of the banks." Not the action of the government, the action of the banks!
Since our civilisation is based on money and no one among us is able to do anything without money, it is obvious that this has everyone at the mercy of banks. It is so true that a bank can literally make somebody out of you financially speaking one day and have you go bankrupt the day after; banks have that power, not only on governments, but also on individuals, businessmen,

June 28, 1971
The Budget-Mr. Caouette
industrialists, etc. who count on bank credit everywhere in Canada for everything. An increase in taxes while decreasing the amount of money available to the taxpayer tightens the bounds of slavery we are subjected to by the banks.
The first clear insight, then, short of inquiring as to the disposal made of taxes, must be of the heavy burden of taxation laid upon us and that directly profits the banks within the banking system.
In considering what disposition is made of the taxes levied we realize that a big portion goes to pay interest on the national debt and, the rest, the bigger portion, pays for social security for those dispossessed through this system. Social welfare recipients are victims of the system and part of the taxes are now used to help those who are deprived in order to pay taxes and interests. A funny system if ever there was one, endorsed by economists who pride themselves in finding solutions.
Mr. Speaker, after the First World War, the national debt of Canada was approximately $1.5 billion. In 1960, it was 12 billion and, in 1971, $24 billion, thus increasing more and more each year. However, the interest this year, according to the new budget, will be $2,030 million. Such is the first statement. We will have a supplementary budget before the end of the year and it will mention another amount to be added to the $2,030 million already announced. That is one reason why Canadians are being deprived of their wealth. In 1971, the debt stands at $24 billion and it goes on increasing. It is likely that 80 per cent of this debt were created through the above-mentioned process, that is, the writing of figures by the bankers or the creation of money by the banks, this money being loaned to the country for the purchase of bonds, Treasury bills, and other securities.
Here is how the situation is analysed in the budget papers and proposals of the Minister of Finance. The deficit of the federal government, in 1961-62, was $791 million. Indeed, until 1971-72, with the exception of 196970 where there was a surplus of $393 million, we have had nothing but deficits. But, in addition to the deficits of $370, $600 or $750 million, the present gross debt of Canada amounts to $42,965,500,000. The increase in our debt, for 1971, amounts to $417 million, and the interest, as I said a while ago, to $2,030 million. This means that we pay $5,561,643 every day, in interest only, on Canada's debt. Five million dollars a day, but that amount is not discussed in Parliament. The Minister of Finance does not speak of it. It is a sacred matter.
Mr. Speaker, no minister dares speak of the $5,561,643 we pay daily in interest. But when mention is made of $500,000 to help the young, the pensioners, the students, then the government keeps saying: "We have no money". We did not hear the Minister of Finance tell us the other day that we have no money to pay $5,561,643 a day in interest. Indeed not, it is a sacred matter.
Mr. Speaker, it is untrue to maintain that this interest is paid to individuals. Half of it is paid to the banking

system, as reported in the table on page 56 of the budget papers. More than half is paid to the banking system.
Mr. Speaker, the table shows that in 1960, the banking system held $1,381 million in treasury bills and that this amount has reached $3,366 million in 1970. An increase of 1,985 million of what? Printed money? Dollars bearing the likeness of the Queen? No, cheques made up by the banking system! It is holding $1,985 million. The government does not mention it. No. They are asking the Canadian people to tighten their belts to pay for the administration of the banking system. That is sacred. Finance must be paid. But people can be left to starve. Yes, mothers and whole families are exposed to extreme misery. But not the financiers! They have to be kept alive, nourished and fattened. We have to work for them. It is the worship the golden calf. That is our system at present.
Mr. Speaker, the banking system which held only $5,802 million of the public debt now holds $10,935 or almost $11 billion, an increase of $5,133 million.
Which means, Mr. Speaker, that within 10 years the banking system doubled its assets in Canadian bonds and treasury bonds, and now holds more than 40 per cent of the debt, while it had only about 34 per cent. It also means that out of the $2 billion Canadian taxpayers will pay in interest this year, the banking system will get more than $800 million, profits drawn out of nothing of about $2.5 million a day for Canadian bankers.
The minister himself admits it as can be seen on page 56 of the Budget Papers, and I quote:
During the past decade, of the $7.9 billion raised by the issue of Government of Canada securities, the banking system, that is the Bank of Canada and the chartered banks, absorbed all the marketable bonds and Treasury bills issued as well as a reduction of over $1 billion in holdings of all others.
Mr. Speaker, that is what the minister said. In other words, the banking system benefits from the billions of dollars paid every year by Canadian taxpayers for debt service.
To say it more clearly, it means that since banks create money or their means of payment out of nothing, except by means of accounts and cheques they draw upon themselves, it enables them to buy treasury bonds and Canada saving bonds with pieces of paper which do not cost them anything. And all the taxes and surtaxes we are paying are used and will be used more and more to pay ever higher annual amounts in tribute money to the banks and to increase the discretionary and totalitarian power they have on the life of everyone, on the life of institutions and governments whatever they may be.
If the Canada bonds, the treasury bills and other securities bought by the banks had all been credited to the Canadian public since 1960, nearly $10 billion, as the Minister of Finance said, would have been capitalized in the name of the Canadian taxpayers. However if all securities had not been registered in the name of the banks since confederation, the national debt would not exist and the national assets of Canadians would be over $42 billion rather than a $42 billion debt. Moreover,
June 28, 1971

instead of paying taxes to reimburse banks and pay them $2 billion in interest each year, Canadians would be paid instead annual dividends of approximately $2,030, million.
For those who find that funny, dividends that is, it is odd that they do not laugh at dividends paid to the banking system. But they would find it strange to pay dividends to Canadians who are building Canada.
Therefore, there would be no more socializing, punitive and tyrannical taxes such as we have under the present financial system, even though the minister boasts of having eased our fiscal burden, reduced or eliminated tax on margarine, etc. In fact, he resorted to all kinds of small measures in an effort to lull the population.
Mr. Speaker, if we were not subjected to the present arbitrary taxes, we could pay national dividends under the Social Credit system we have been urging-at all times and not only before an election-the elected government to establish in order to administer on the basis of the people's needs and our ability to bring them security in freedom.
It is along the lines of that program that for many years we have been working, explaining and stating the Social Credit financial theory to the House.
Mr. Speaker, the day will come and may be closer at hand than we think, when we will have to choose between two things: either to put the financial system in the service of man, or communism, confusion, revolution, the effects of which are beginning to be felt in various areas of Canada.
There is a limit to the sufferings and hardships which may be imposed on people who want to live, to develop, to build a national heritage which really belongs to them. There is a limit to the sacrifices forever to be imposed in the interest of financiers, the only ones who do not suffer hardships in Canada!
Mr. Speaker, let us try and prevent people's sufferings. Let us give financiers a taste of misery and put money in the service of the people in our country, Canada.

speakeroldname: Mr. Alastair Gillespie (Parliamentary Secretary to President of the Treasury Board):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Treasury Board
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in rising to take part in this debate I recognize it as a rather historic occasion; it might even be described as a watershed in the process of government. I am referring in particular to the process of participation which is coming, if not at least to a close, close to a close in this debate and to a close in the clause by clause examination in which we will participate this September.
Before entering into my speech I should like to comment on one or two things that the hon. member for Temiscamingue (Mr. Caouette) said in his speech to which I listened with considerable interest a moment ago. I suppose that if I had to put it down in a few words I would say that it was an interesting voyage into the outer space of high finance. For me it was too far out, a little too high. He made such statements as that if we were to adopt his policies, there would be no national 24171-471
The Budget-Mr. Gillespie
debt at all. He even went so far as to suggest that those who lend their money to the banks-most of his speech was devoted to a discussion of the importance of the banking system in financing our affairs today-would do so without requiring any interest payment on their savings. Surely this tests our credibility too far. Also, in the early part of his speech he referred to the new tax legislation and the proposals as they might affect Canadians on lower incomes. He seemed to ignore some of the statistics and figures that have been presented by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Benson) in his budget speech a week ago Friday. I should like to remind the hon. member for Temiscamingue that under these proposals, one million Canadians would be taken off the tax rolls altogether, and there would be a further 4,700,000 Canadians who would have their taxes reduced. Those are significant and important figures, and I think that the hon. member for Temiscamingue should be reminded of them.
I do not propose in my speech today to recite the various provisions of the tax legislation-others have already done so very competently. The Minister of Finance, the able, affable, persistent, flexible and very responsive Minister of Finance, took two hours to set before the House the largest, the most complete set of tax proposals that this House has ever considered. The hon. member for Grenville-Carleton (Mr. Blair) in his speech dealt with the question of reform versus tax change. He recited case by case the reform elements in this package of new tax legislation. He was followed by the incisive and, to my view, the very clearminded hon. member for Don Valley (Mr. Kaplan) who reminded the hon. member for Edmonton West (Mr. Lambert), the financial critic of the Conservative party, that equity is an important part of a tax system. If there are only two pillars in the tax system, this would be the second pillar. The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance, the hon. member for Calgary South (Mr. Mahoney), dealt in his lengthy speech with the specific points of the tax legislation. It is unnecessary for me to go over that ground again.

speechtext: Who wrote his speech?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Treasury Board
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
The other person whom I would like to mention at this juncture is the hon. member for Gatineau (Mr. Clermont) who was chairman of the House of Commons Finance Committee, a man who more than most would understand and have experienced the process of participation-the able, respected member for Gatineau who took the committee through the most exhaustive series of hearings that any parliamentary committee, in my knowledge, has been exposed to.
It is not my intention to go through the provisions of this tax legislation, as I have already indicated, nor is it my intention to deal with the budget provisions as distinct from the tax legislation provisions, other than to observe that our critics seemed to have difficulty in finding something to attack. They have had considerable difficulty in swallowing the relief from the 3 per cent surcharge. They seemed to have accepted the idea of not

June 28, 1971
The Budget-Mr. Gillespie
taxing those with a taxable income of less than $500 at the lower income level. They have accepted it but they do not seem to be able to find what they are looking for, that is, some way to say that this is a suggestion that they had made. Equally, they have had difficulty in dealing with the relief from excise tax of the electronic industry and the relief from sales tax on margarine. I think that perhaps the House has already recognized that these are important measures, well designed to help the economy forward, as the Finance Minister said, over any pause that might develop.
Perhaps the best compliment that has been paid to us was paid by the hon. member for Prince Edward-Has-tings (Mr. Hees). He has a good, straightforward view of many things. The simpler the better for the hon. member for Prince Edward-Hastings. It was his view that this must be an election budget because it was just too good. Translated into what might be described as Prince Edward-Hastings-'ees, "It's a damned good budget, baby." There is one thing about the hon. member for Prince Edward-Hastings. He does not like to one-upped. He produced what he thought would be his own best design for an election budget. He would reduce income taxes by 10 per cent right across the piece.
l
Mr. Speaker, what I want to do, as I have indicated, is talk about the process of participation which the tax legislation is now rapidly concluding. It is pretty obvious, as we cast our minds back over a period of two years, that the Tories have never really understood the process. It is not in their tradition, and I suppose we should not say that this is a surprise. The idea of participation does not come naturally to the Conservative party. It also perhaps explains why the Tories are now having so much difficulty in making up their minds as to whether they should try to take some credit for the tax legislation or whether they should criticize it. In my view they have not done either very well, which I suppose is also in the Conservative tradition.
They have tried to suggest to us that this is not reform at all, that it is tax change. Well of course it is tax change because there is no reform unless there is change, and the important thing, Mr. Speaker, is that these are important changes. One has only got to look over the list to see how important they are and to realize that it is fundamental and comprehensive reform.
They have criticized this tax legislation as too long in coming. Well, let me remind them that they started the process in 1962.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Are you giving any credit for that?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Treasury Board
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I do. I think that was a wise decision. Your government of the day and subsequent Liberal governments have dealt with this issue started in 1962. But at various points in the last two years the Conservatives have had trouble wondering whether we were going too fast or too slow.
As I recall it, on one occasion last year, early in the year, the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Stanfield) said
that we should withdraw the white paper. For him this was not participation. He wanted to withdraw it and start all over again. Later in the year their financial critic, a member of the House of Commons Finance Committee, stated he felt we were going too fast. He even accused us of closure, of using the guillotine, and he called a press conference to tell the Canadian people that the Liberals were trying to close off debate, that they were trying in some way to guillotine the whole process of participation.
More recently the Leader of the Opposition stated that this new tax legislation lacks credibility. These are his words. Anyone who has read this new tax legislation, anyone who has looked at it, who has listened to the comments, must say that that criticism lacks credibility.
I would like to go back then to the process itself and just remind hon. members opposite that on November 5, 1969, when the Minister of Finance tabled his white paper, in effect he said to the Canadian people, "Give us your views. Play a part in helping us to reform the tax system." What did the Leader of the Opposition say, Mr. Speaker? He said, "Withdraw the document"! He did not understand participation.
More recently he has taken another tack. When this new tax legislation was presented he thought that perhaps he should change his view and he said, "Now the government is backtracking." Those are his words. He never understood the process of participation. Perhaps this is not surprising. After all, his chief financial critic did not either. He, on one occasion, seemed to echo his leader's position that the government should withdraw the white paper. That was earlier last year, although it was not always certain that that was his position. Then, as I have indicated, last June he called a press conference to say that the Liberals were trying to move too fast in bringing the participation process to a useful and constructive conclusion. He accused us of all sorts of things, of the guillotine, of closure, of making the committee hearings a sham.
In Victoria, about a year ago, when the Finance Committee held its final public hearings, that is, public hearings to receive briefs from the private sector, what did the hon. member for Edmonton West do? He rushed to the press again and called another press conference. This time he accused the Liberal members of the committee of all sorts of things, of being about to ram through the tax legislation. He stated that he thought it very likely that they would receive their orders and act in some way as if they were not free men. He even seemed to suggest that the legislation was then already being drafted. I do not think that he understood the process of participation.
And when the Commons committee completed its report during the summer of last year, what did the hon. member for Edmonton West do, and how did he advise his Conservative colleagues on that committee? Again he showed that he did not understand the process of participation. He again showed that he was not able to make up his mind. Neither he nor his colleagues voted to support the House of Commons committee report or to reject it. Mr. Speaker, they could not make up their minds.
