speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Treasury Board
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I would be prepared to accept a question at the end of my remarks.
I would now like to turn to the thrust of the tax legislation proposals. The first point which needs to be made is that the Tory critics appear to have grudgingly approved the higher exemptions for personal taxes, and I say grudgingly because the hon. member for Edmonton West seemed to dispose of equity as if it was not important.
On this point he was reminded by the hon. member for Don Valley that equity has to be a cardinal, a main p'.llar of any taxation system, and indeed it is of this tax legislation. The Leader of the Opposition seemed to acknowledge that lower taxation for wage and salary earners, except for single persons with incomes over $8,000 a year, was a good thing. But there was some difficulty in understanding his arguments about elasticity. He acknowledged the importance of a capital gains tax. These, I think, are all pluses. He seemed to approve that the measures to assist small business were good, but I have looked through the speeches of the hon. members I have mentioned, the Leader of the Opposition and the hon. member for Edmonton West, and I am not clear on their position with respect to small business. I give them the benefit of the doubt, however, Mr. Speaker.
I think it is worth mentioning here that under these new provisions there will be a saving of $2,500 on the first $50,000 taxable income. Under the new proposals there will be a low rate of 25 per cent on the first $50,000 of taxable income, which is $12,500. Under the previous arrangement there was a low level tax of 21 per cent on the first $35,000, which is $7,500, and an additional tax of 50 per cent or slightly over on the next $15,000, which is again in the order of $7,500. So taxes under our present system are $15,000 on the first $50,000 and under the proposed system they will be $12,500.
I have looked in vain for a statement from the members opposite on the reduction of corporate taxes to 46 per cent. Do hon. members approve of this particular incentive to the corporate sector? Nor have hon. members opposite had much to say about the provisions to foster Canadian ownership. I put it to them, Mr. Speaker, where do they stand on these provisions?

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Where do you stand?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Treasury Board
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Right behind them.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: How far?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Treasury Board
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Let me say in that connection, Mr. Speaker, that there are some important changes which go further than the hon. members opposite have noted here. One is with respect to the position of Canadian based multinational corporations. Let me take a moment to review some of these provisions which are going to assist potential Canadian based multinational corporations and which will assist mature Canadian based multinational
The Budget-Mr. Gillespie
corporations. On the potential side there are two things in particular and one is a low rate for the small corporation. If a foreign corporation purchases a small Canadian corporation which has enjoyed the benefit of the low rate of taxes on the first $50,000 of taxable income it will have to pay back the tax savings earned by that small corporation. A Canadian corporation will not have to. Similarly, interest charges are now deductible to Canadian purchasers. This will place the potential Canadian based multinational corporation on the same basis as foreign corporations.
The provisions with respect to pension funds and with respect to dividend tax credits should materially assist the financing of mature Canadian based multinational corporations by Canadians. Under the new tax legislation proposals, foreign source dividend income will be treated on the same basis as it is now and not on the basis proposed in the white paper. The treatment of foreign source income is a very complicated area as is the question of dividend income, income from operations and passive income. I do not propose to go further than to say that this will require considerable study by the House. I think it is most important that we recognize that Canadian based multinational corporations should be able to compete on an equal basis with multinational corporations in third markets.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Canadian based or Canadian owned?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Treasury Board
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Canadian controlled, Canadian based, multinational corporations.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Canadian owned?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Treasury Board
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Canadian controlled.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: There is quite a difference.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Treasury Board
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Canadian controlled with Canadian
shareholders, Mr. Speaker. Let me deal with some of the NDP positions. They have just recently started to show an interest in my remarks, Mr. Speaker.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Corporate chicanery.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Treasury Board
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
There are two particular things which seem to characterize the remarks of the hon. members opposite and both of them, I think, involve contradictions. In their remarks they seem to be wedded to the Carter commission proposals. For instance, they seem to have forgotten that the royal commission proposals were a package and that with full capital gains there was full integration. We have heard a great deal to the effect that these proposals only provide for the taxing of half capital gains and that it should have been full capital gains.
We have heard nothing about the fact that the integration proposals of Carter would mean the following sort of thing if they were accepted alongside. Under the Carter commission proposals dividend income would not have been taxable in the hands of individuals; dividend income would not have been taxable if first taxed as corporate income. You would have seen individuals with a dividend income of $100,000 a year paying no tax. Is this what the NDP want? If they want Carter that is

June 28, 1971
The Budget-Mr. Hellyer
what they get. It is time they reread Carter to find out what he recommended. They see with one eye and they see only half a package. They have a half vast view.
The NDP also talked about neutrality. If they were to apply the principle of neutrality would they have lifted completely the low rate of tax for small business? Do they understand what direct investment means? Do they understand natural resources are developed by direct investment, that direct investment is the name of the game? Do they think that a natural resource company interested in development is likely to go into the electronic business? Fiscal measures used selectively, on NDP position, are, of course, the very opposite of neutral. Out of the window goes the principle of neutrality.
They are also contradictory in another area, Mr. Speaker, and this is the NDP attitude toward inflation and particularly toward the government voluntary restraint program. "Let's encourage those who are negotiating for higher incomes", seems to be their attitude. Then when costs and prices go up and when they affect people on fixed incomes they berate the government for paying no attention to those people. They cannot have it both ways, Mr. Speaker. It is a bankrupt policy-a policy of contradiction.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Are you talking about the government policy for unemployment?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Treasury Board
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, in concluding-

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Good.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Treasury Board
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: -I should like to run over the criteria of a good tax system and the tests that should be applied to a good tax system. Five were set forth by the Minister of Finance and they were growth, equity, to close abuses and loopholes, to provide for administrative efficiency, economy and, justice. The fifth is compatibility of provincial systems. I think the tax legislation which we will be considering in detail meets those tests, Mr. Speaker, but there is a sixth and it is implied. It is that any tax system must meet national objectives. I think this tax legislation does meet a national objective. It is a move in the right direction of stimulating Canadian ownership. I do not pretend that by themselves these provisions are enough. They are not, and like many other members of the House I am anxiously waiting, perhaps even a little impatiently, for the announcement of the policy of the government on foreign ownership.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Yes, we have waited a long time.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Treasury Board
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: I think the process of participation which I have tried to review, Mr. Speaker, has shown that this exercise will work. I think that this patricular legislation is a victory for the people of Canada, for the process of participation, and for common sense.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: First of all, Mr. Speaker-

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: We will hear truth now, unbiased truth.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: First, Mr. Speaker, I want to congratulate the government on presenting a budget which was so much better than anyone expected that they deserve commendation.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: One could nitpick, of course, but this is not the time for nitpicking. In normal times the budget could only be described as good by a normal observer. But these are not normal times, Mr. Speaker. The Canadian economy is alive, but sick.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: It is very, very sick.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
And what the budget speech failed to tell us was how we got into this mess in the first place. Nor did it tell us how to get out of it. These are omissions of staggering proportions.
The fact is, Mr. Speaker, that the government's economic policies are tearing the country apart. In my whole life I have never seen so much bickering, dissatisfaction and frustration.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Are you listening, Alastair?

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: That is evident everywhere except among the naive, the well fed and the complacent.

speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader; Whip of the N.D.P.
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: That is the cabinet.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Surely the decision of the Quebec government to reject the constitutional charter must not be interpreted only as an expression of Quebec nationalism; it must be interpreted, partly at least, as a reaction to the massive intrusion of the federal government into areas of provincial jurisdiction in the 1960's.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: It is interesting to note, Mr. Speaker, that although the people of Quebec seem to want a greater degree of control over their own affairs, particularly those involving social security, the interests of individual Quebeckers seem to be very similar to those of people in other parts of the country. On the basis of sample memberships in Action Canada-

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: What's that?

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: -may I say that 45 per cent of the membership in Quebec indicate that unemployment is the matter of primary concern to them.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Progressive Conservative Party
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Is the government listening?

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
The second and third matters of concern, in order of priority, are inflation and tax reform. Of the people of Quebec who have joined Action Canada, only 2 per cent have indicated that constitutional reform and only 3 per cent have indicated that federal-provincial relations were their first concerns.
June 28. 1971

The Prairie provinces and British Columbia are unhappy too. Whether or not it is fair to interrupt the Saskatchewan vote as a rejection in part of Ottawa's agricultural policies, the fact remains that there is a great deal of dissatisfaction in Canada's western provinces.

speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader; Whip of the N.D.P.
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: They are dissatisfied with Ottawa.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Ontario, too, is losing patience with Ottawa. The people of this province are getting fed up with paying exorbitant taxes to finance harebrained, bureaucratic decisions in the field of regional development and some-I underline "some"-Opportunities for Youth projects. They would not mind if the programs were producing the desired benefits in relation to cost. However, in many cases they are not doing that. In many cases they just transfer unemployment from one geographical location to another without improving the overall situation significantly.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: They transfer unemployment even within the same areas.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I suspect that the Atlantic provinces are unhappy too. They certainly should be, with the level of unemployment existing there. This is a tragic situation and one that is thoroughly unacceptable in a so-called civilized society. The whole problem relates back to the management of our economy.
It is not the system that is at fault, Mr. Speaker; it is the managers. It is not imported unemployment and misery that we are suffering from; it is the home-grown variety. It is not the ravages of famine or war that we are suffering from; it is the consequences of economic mismanagement which can only be described as inhumane and unintelligent. The number of unemployed persons is still ridiculously high. An improvement of a fraction of a percentage point is little comfort to the hundreds of thousands of human beings who are still without work.
A few days ago when I was visiting Winnipeg I was driven to the airport by a young man. I asked him if he was a student. He replied that, no, he was a graduate. He had graduated in chemical engineering and was unable to find employment of any kind in his own field. Consequently he took a position driving a taxi. I also received a letter a few days ago from a woods product scientist. This man lost his job as a result of the contraction in the pulp industry and was unable to find any kind of useful employment in his own field in this great country. That is a tragic reflection of the opportunities available for people of energy and education who want to create a better society. These people have one thing in common- a feeling of hopelessness and frustration because they are the hapless victims of the way the system is being operated. They have the ability to work. They have the desire to work and they have the qualifications for contributing much to this great country. Yet for reasons beyond their control they are not able to participate in a meaningful way in our economy. Young people prepare themselves to contribute, to produce and to be productive
The Budget-Mr. Hellyer
and then, through no fault of their own, they are unable to do so. That is probably the greatest tragedy that can befall a nation.
In budgeting for a large deficit the government seems to be following the 30-year old edict of Lord Keynes. One wonders when revenues will be adequate to meet the needs of a voracious government. It is difficult to be optimistic in the face of the fact that interest on the public debt alone has increased by more than 200 per cent in 15 years.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: That is shocking.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
That is galloping inflation. Nor is the end in sight. What about the extra $100 million required for the proposed family allowance revisions and what about the several hundred million dollars that will be required for the new Unemployment Insurance Act? Where will that money come from?
To speak of the unemployment insurance bill, Mr. Speaker, raises the specter of an enormous credibility gap. Without reflecting on the decision taken by the House, I think it might be worth while to examine that new act for evidence of a monumental snow job.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Oh, oh!

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: First of all, it appears that we were deceived by the government which held that the proposal was a bona fide insurance scheme that will give rise to virtually the same cost to the government as the previous act did. This contention was never supported by the facts. No actuarial report was produced. I suspect the reason was that none exists. Reference was made to a consultant's report by Urwick, Currie. That too has not been made public. Why? Are the public not capable of comprehending?

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Order, please. It being one o'clock I do now leave the chair.
At one o'clock the House took recess.

AFTER RECESS

The House resumed at 2 p.m.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
At one o'clock, Mr. Speaker, I was discussing the unemployment insurance bill and the lack of a proper actuarial report in respect of it. I was asking, why the secret? I presume that if a proper actuarial basis existed in support of the government's case that it would have been made public. I can only assume that the lack of public presentation of such a report indicates that there is none in fact. The sickness and pregnancy benefits were guesses. The alleged benefits due to the extension of the waiting period and the elimination of seasonal benefits are largely fictional.
Apart from the sloppiness of the mathematics, Mr. Speaker, a fundamental objection must be the continued emphasis of unemployment insurance or welfare as a

June 28, 1971
The Budget-Mr. Hellyer
substitute for jobs. Everyone agrees that individuals should be adequately compensated when jobs are not available through no fault of their own. That is fundamental. But jobs should be available. It should be a man's inalienable right to work if he wants to work. In our kind of society, we should see that that fundamental right is guaranteed. The present situation is not necessary. It is a result of a deliberate policy on the part of the government to fight inflation by nineteenth century methods.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Hear, hear.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
For support of the suggestion that we could have had full employment in Canada, one need only look at the experience in other western countries. There is full employment in Japan, Germany, Switzerland, the Scandinavian countries, Australia and New Zealand. In fact, in almost every western country, with the exception of the United States, Canada, and to a certain extent Great Britain, full employment policies are being pursued. In Canada, we have mismanaged our economy. The consequences for hundreds of thousands of our citizens in human terms are beyond description.
In recent weeks I have received literally hundreds of letters from unemployed people. In not one single case did they ask for higher unemployment insurance benefits. Almost universally and without exception they suggested that they wanted employment. They wanted work. They want to use their talents, strength and energy to help build a better Canada.
A profound objection to the Unemployment Insurance Act and the minister's budget is the institutionalizing of unemployment. By inference at least. In the Unemployment Insurance Act, and in all of the other acts and statements of the government at the present time, we are being led to believe that 4 per cent unemployment is to be considered normal. The consistent use of this figure by the government must be considered part of the conditioning process to get the public used to the idea of chronic unemployment. It is not good enough. In fact, it is preposterous. The idea must be vigorously rejected. On June 19, the Toronto Star suggested that one of the minister's officials used the figure of 5 per cent unemployment as a target figure. That is even more preposterous. I hope the minister will lose no time in denying the validity of that idea, if he has not already done so.
In underestimating the cost in future tax increases required for unemployment insurance by an order of 8 or 10, the government is not levelling with the people. In following this course, it raises the question of the credibility of all its budgetary proposals. Have budgetary revenues been over-estimated and, if so, by how much? As a matter of fact, if private industry were to make a presentation to the public which was so inaccurate,-

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: They would go to jail.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
-the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs (Mr. Basford) would lay charges. It is the old shell game. Watch closely for the figures are quicker than the eye. The public gets a view of the benefits before the
election. It gets the fantastic bill and higher taxes afterward.
If inflation rises to expectant levels next winter, even the minor benefits to the little people will be unceremoniously wiped out. We must end these policies that tear the country apart. They are not good enough. The people want jobs, stable prices and lower taxes than are in existence at the present time, because in many cases the pressure is becoming too great. These are not unreasonable expectations, Mr. Speaker. It would be different if such achievements were beyond our capacity, but that is not the case. We in Canada have fantastic resources, both human and material. All we have to do is to put them to work in an intelligent way. This is why we cannot blame the people for wanting more. We have raised their expectations but the realization is incompatible with those expectations. The people now want changes in government policy. Instead of minor tinkering, they want to know how to solve the present situation in which they find themselves, to the point where every Canadian who wants to work is able to work: where every Canadian who retires with a pension of $2,000 a year will know that his pension will buy just as much five years later as at the time of retirement; where every Canadian who is taxed to death on his real estate and in other ways will know that somehow he will be able to get by and raise his family with some sort of dignity and decency. These are not unreasonable suggestions or expectations for a country as great at this, but we have to change our policies very dramatically and substantially if we are to provide our people with what they want and deserve.
The Minister of Finance concluded his speech by saying that we are on course. On course for where, Mr. Speaker? Niagara Falls? Earlier the minister said that the data that he had produced suggests that, while we cannot insulate ourselves from the pervasive impact of economic influences from the United States, we have it in our hands to achieve a somewhat better performance if we have the wisdom and the will to do so. With that masterpiece of understatement I agree, Mr. Speaker, so let us get at it.

speakeroldname: Mr. E. B. Osier (Winnipeg South Centre):
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I want to say a few words on the budget and I hope hon. members will give me their indulgence since my usual bull voice has become even more "bully" and it may be difficult to get across what I want to say.
At the outset, and without being in any way personal- because I do not intend to be personal about a man whom I like and admire greatly-I regret that the hon. member for Trinity (Mr. Hellyer) did not specify in his speech that he was a minister, and a very senior minister, of a government that fought an election, at least in part, on the issue of inflation and how to attack it. I might add that to my knowledge he never opened his mouth in caucus against the methods being used to fight inflation. Therefore, having heard his speech, it is a little difficult not to make those observations. Otherwise I

June 28, 1971

thought he made a constructive contribution to the debate.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: He has seen the light.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
He may have seen the light, but I am afraid he should have had his dark glasses on because it has been a little too dazzling for him to gaze upon.
We have before us a proposed budget and a series of documents containing provisions of legislation that is about to be introduced to reform personal and corporate income taxes. These are, as other speakers have pointed out, quite separate things. Neither the budget nor the proposed provisions for tax reform are perfect, but, then, nothing in this world ever is perfect. In my opinion, the comments we have heard so far from the official opposition and the spokesmen for the NDP, and also for those who are playing "rover" on their own, fall far short of anything to be expected of normally competent men in this imperfect world.
As for Conservative reaction, I looked up some words of Sir Walter Raleigh, who was quite a figure a few hundred years ago, who said something that might sum up the comments of Conservative members. He said: "Fain would I, but I dare not". As for the reaction of the NDP, in view of the problems that they have been experiencing with the "Waffle", I again turn to the words of Sir Walter Raleigh, who said: "I dare, and yet I may not".
This government can dare, Mr. Speaker, and it has dared. In the first instance, it has dared to take up the challenge of tax reform and to engage in dialogue with the people before coming to any decisions. In the second instance, it has dared to heed the will of the people and to modify its own views. Finally, it has drafted legislation for this Parliament to consider and to act upon. Would the NDP have taken this action? Has it ever managed to bring itself to admit that it may not be all wise in the management of the people's affairs? Would it have changed direction in the slightest degree in public?
We who sit to your right, Mr. Speaker, are often accused by the scribes and the pharisees on the other side of the House of being arrogant, heartless and technocratic in our approach to all problems. Indeed, technocratic is a favourite word to be found in the glossary of gall-soaked adjectives that the new leader of the NDP inherited from the old leader. Yet, in spite of this, we are now condemned for modifying our original proposals. We may be arrogant in the eyes of some, Mr. Speaker, but we are not afraid to try to meet problems. Nor are we afraid to admit that when a man tries to do something meaningful he does run the risk of making some mistakes. We may be heartless, Mr. Speaker, but we do have sufficient courage and concern to lay our necks on the line and to adopt new policies in our efforts to find new solutions to age old problems of equity and growth.
The hon. member for Waterloo (Mr. Saltsman) made much of the so-called bribes to businessmen that he said were contained in our proposals for tax reform. To my mind the hon. member for Don Valley (Mr. Kaplan) effectively demolished his reasoning on this subject. I 24171-48
The Budget-Mr. Osier
would merely like to add that the Schreyer government in Manitoba seems more inclined to go along with this government's reasoning than do the NDP members of this House.
In the speech from the throne which the present government of Manitoba delivered this year, there were three interesting items that indicated to me that that government was at least trying to head in the same direction as this government. The first item is as follows:
Programs for economic and industrial development will be focussed primarily on activities which will not only increase average per capita income, but will also improve the distribution of that income among the population.
The second item is this:
My Ministers inform me also that plans have been made to provide for more effective recognition of the potential of small business through a small business loans operation as an integral part of the Manitoba Development Corporation.
Lastly, item No. 3 reads:
You will be asked to approve of expenditures for the purpose of the creation of a mineral exploration company which will be able to embark on programs to discover viable Manitoba resources either on its own initiative, or in partnership with other exploration companies.
It is pretty strong meat for social democrats to admit that they will be dealing with business people who may have ideas and can help them achieve their objectives. It is too bad that the members of that party in this House do not take a leaf from the book of the members of their party in Manitoba and be a little more realistic in their approach to matters, instead of talking of bribing businessmen. The hon. member for Waterloo might well brief himself on what his social democratic confreres are attempting to do about stimulating business in Manitoba before he denounces the government party in this House for trying to do the same thing.
There is nothing much to say about the remarks of the members of the official opposition. They are still impaled on the fence that they spent last year constructing with a melange of old driftwood and a few rusty nails. I think it was the week before last that the leader of the Progressive Conservatives is reputed to have said that the government has "the smell of fatigue and collapse of a loser's locker room". At least, that is what he is alleged to have said. I can only add that he ought to recognize the aroma because he has smelled it often enough; and behind the lockers in his locker room I caution him to watch out for shadowy figures clutching the assassin's knife. I have played on many a team that has lost a game. I was even in an air force once that lost a battle or two. But, I have never smelled the smell of "a loser's locker room" and I am certainly not smelling it now. I think the hon. gentleman must have been standing with his back to the wind when he recorded those immortal words.
The business of the government is to govern, and it requires courage to govern in this day and age of changing values and problems of unprecedented gravity. It requires the courage to try and the courage to admit the

June 28, 1971
The Budget-Mr. Osier
possibility that one may make mistakes. The people of Canada are the ones who must ultimately decide this issue. The people of Canada are fair-minded; they admire courage and, according to much of the mail I receive, it would appear they are fed up with the carping, unproductive criticism we hear so often in this House.
We have two things here, a budget and proposed measures for tax reform. The budget seems to me to be a good one. We have the elimination of the 3 per cent surtax, new personal exemptions and reductions in sales and excise taxes, all of which amount to a little over $200 million being injected into the economy during the next half of this year. We have $650 million more put into the economy as a result of government spending delayed from the winter, and $400 million in new programs intended for 1971-72.
This should further encourage demand for consumer durable goods, which already seems to be on the rise. I understand retail sales have increased by 4.5 per cent from March to April with an underlying trend in relation to prices, being about 3 per cent more per year. So, real growth this year should be determined at the rate of 5 per cent to 5.5 per cent. In any event, we are gaining in productivity.
The elimination of tax uncertainty should provide business with enough encouragement to stimulate its own capital investment program. Manufacturing activity appears to be picking up in spite of the fact that over-all unemployment remains regrettably high. There were
57,000	new jobs in manufacturing in May and 67,000 new jobs in the construction industry in that same month, and the rate of unemployment is going down.
Hopefully the slight trend for imports to climb faster than exports will not persist, but we must continue our efforts to sell to customers other than the United States. Hopefully too, the downward trend in the value of the Canadian dollar will continue, because this will not only stimulate industry, it will free Canadian funds for government cash requirements in Canada and reduce the necessity for having to go to the bond market.
As for tax reform, the proposal brought forward by this government shows concern both for people as individuals and the economic machinery required to fulfil their needs. The NDP sound sometimes as if this economic machinery should be looked upon as a disease unless it is owned by the state. In a country like Canada you Cannot have equity for an increasing population unless you also have economic growth. You cannot have growth at anywhere near the rate required to increase real per capita income and consumption unless the rate of capital accumulation, and of productive improvement, matches the expectations of the people.
The greatest achievements of the government's reform plan are the increased personal exemptions, the deductibility of child care expenses for working mothers, the introduction of income averaging for those who have fluctuating incomes or who receive large lump sum payments such as capital gains, the major increases in deductibility of contributions to pension plans, the deductibility of an employee's cost of earning his living,
the deductibility of an employee's moving expenses, the increased exemptions for those over the age of 65, and the increase of deductible gifts to charitable organizations from 10 per cent to 20 per cent of one's income. The government has achieved these things for individuals without weakening the economic machinery required if this land of ours is not to stagnate. It is to be hoped that the provinces will refrain from jumping in to fill the reductions in the federal tax load with new provincial taxes. To prevent this, people must be as vigilant and as vociferous toward their provincial governments as they have been in the past year toward the federal government and its white paper proposals.
Premier Schreyer of Manitoba is reputed to have already said the federal tax system would reduce Manitoba's tax revenues, and that he will have to consider levying a provincial estate tax and increase the retail sales tax. He said this, in spite of the fact the federal government has guaranteed that provinces will not suffer a revenue drop, or if they do that Ottawa will make it up. He has said this, too, in spite of the fact the provinces will have new revenue from their share of the new capital gains tax and their increased taxing right over mineral companies. This will give them an extra 15 per cent. One can only wonder about a statement or an attitude like this, especially when one suspects that Manitoba's taxes were bound to go up anyway in order to fulfil the recent promises of its politicians. These promises were made even before they knew anything about the federal government proposals.
It is to be hoped that provincial governments will follow the federal lead toward tax relief instead of following this predicted road. For example, federal tax reform proposals will result in the elimination of tax for all couples who are 65 years of age and older on their income up to $3,600. It would be logical for the provinces to now reduce the real property tax for home owners in the same age group, that is if they are as socially minded as they claim.
Lastly, it is to be hoped that efforts will be intensified to reduce or at least check the rate of expansion of the federal budget, and that the federal authority, now that it has created a new tax framework, will persist in its search for a truly effective way of stimulating development in slow-growth areas. Will the way not soon be open to allow tax incentives to eliminate regional disparity?
It seems to me the proposals which will gradually alter the basis for taxation of the mining and petroleum industries might provide some room for tax incentives to manufacturing and service industries in the less dynamic regions of Canada. Must we sit by while Toronto, Montreal and Vancouver become overcrowded monstrosities unfit to live in and the rest of the country becomes an unpopulated desert? There is nothing personal in my reference to Montreal, Toronto and Vancouver. But there are predictions that they are going to grow into monstrosities unless something is done. Must we stand by while they become such monstrosities? I certainly hope we will not have to do this. I feel the federal government should continue vigorously to pursue a goal of regional

June 28, 1971

equality of opportunity. I certainly hope it will do what it must in respect of tax concessions and exemptions to gain such an end.
I am happy to note that the federal government plans to encourage Canadian saving and investment. I am not one of those who has a psychopathic hatred of foreign investment, particularly of the non-shareholding kind. But it seems to me we should not forever depend on foreign sources of savings, because capital inflows from abroad may cease to flow in this capital-poor world in which we live, or at least cease in terms that would be acceptable to us.
Finally, I must repeat that the government's proposal strikes a workable balance between equity and growth. We need growth in order to provide equity. We need equity to ensure a continued orderly function in our society. This must surely be the only foundation on which growth itself can be achieved. Thus equity and growth are complementary, not opposing factors in the equation. Thus both should be maximized to as great an extent as possible by government tax policy. I believe what we see is a maximizing and very acceptable compromise, following a year and a half consideration of the white paper and budget proposals.
Before I sit down, I should like to congratulate the House of Commons and Senate committees for the exhaustive and very intelligent work they performed for over a year and a half. Let me congratulate the government, and especially the Minister of Finance (Mr. Benson), for being open-minded enough to look in a neutral and fair way at the proposals which came from these sources. Let me congratulate the government itself for being big enough to come out with this reform proposal now tabled for the consideration of this House.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, when I look at this budget and the so-called reforms in the tax structure, I must come to the conclusion that western Canada once again is to suffer from eastern domination. What seems to me to be a total lack of regard for the western economy, the farm situation and western development, will once again breed distrust and suspicion among westerners. I am disgusted at this government for allowing the economy of Western Canada to reach the stage it has. In my opinion, the effect of this budget has been magnified. It will do little for economic expansion in western Canada. I cannot see it reducing unemployment but, along with other government controls, I can see it having a highly inflationary effect. The so-called tax reform fails to take into account the plight of the small farmer. I also feel that the capital gains tax is discriminatory to the owners of small businesses and farmers.
One cannot necessarily make a blanket attack on all the budget proposals but neither can they be hailed as the great tax reforms they have been called. These tax reform proposals must be a betrayal of one of the principles of true tax reform, the principle of equity. An equitable system, I believe, should take into account regional disparities, the nature of certain industries and the unequal burdens created by the present tax system.
24171-48J
The Budget-Mr. Murta
In my opinion, this must be labelled an eastern budget. As are most budgets, it was designed by an easterner for the easterner. I must say my greatest hope is that some day we will have a budget which will take into account all of Canada rather than Ontario and Quebec.
I must comment on the general feeling which is growing in western Canada, and then perhaps the minister will understand why the budget fails to impress anyone from that area. Contrary to popular eastern belief, the prairie farmer is not fabricating his complaints. He might perhaps be compared to those in Quebec who seek to preserve and safeguard their culture. The western farmer desires to preserve a way of life, his way of life, and it seems to him today that this government, for some unknown reason, wishes to drive him from his land.
The events of the past five years would almost cause any farmer to think that his demise is a definite part of government policy. Historically, the prairie farmer has had much to complain about, but his complaints never seem to be heard. In fact, they have been totally ignored since this government has come into power. It sounds very dramatic to accuse the government of a definite anti-farm and anti-west policy, Mr. Speaker, but one must eventually come to this conclusion after years of neglect and abuse. I could go into a monologue on discriminatory freight rates, high tariffs to protect the uncompetitive eastern industrialists, lack lustre attempts by the eastern bureaucrats to sell our agricultural products and now, to top if off, the efforts of the provinces of Ontario and Quebec to restrict our agricultural produce from entering their provinces, the latest restriction being on eggs. I would suggest to the minister that he come to rural Manitoba to see the situation for himself, so that he might better understand what I am talking about.
If one travelled through southern Manitoba, he would soon see the shocking situation that is developing. There is a trend, which if not arrested, could leave the countryside in economic shambles. The farmers are going further and further into debt, municipalities are confronted with increases in tax arrears and the people are becoming frustrated and resentful about their lot. City dwellers today may be concerned about inflation and unemployment, but the farmer is concerned about his whole way of life. He sees his costs rising, due in large measure to the ever-increasing wage demands of labour, and his income dropping. He is confronted with property taxes which in many cases run into thousands of dollars and is increasingly hard pressed to find money to pay them. He sees his education taxes, over which he has no control, assuming mountainous proportions. He wonders how long he can hold out in the face of these built-in expenses. He is increasingly resentful of government regulation and control at both the federal and provincial levels. One farmer expressed it in this way. He said it is getting to the point where he might as well be nothing more than a hired man on his own farm because as a hired man, he would be better paid.
Welfare is a live issue in rural Manitoba today, and in most of rural Canada. The hard pressed farmer is bitter and resentful about contributing to welfare costs for people who he believes are faced with fewer real mone-

June 28, 1971
The Budget-Mr. Murta
tary problems than he is. That is the situation in rural Manitoba. It is a situation which has ramifications in every phase of rural life, social, agriculture, economic and political.
A good measure of eastern affluence results from the fact that the non-industrial provinces are forced to buy their consumer goods from the eastern industrialists. It is not only time for this affluence to be shared, but for the development of a western policy. This budget gives no relief to the ailing agricultural industry. It will not relieve the tax burden on the farmer or the small businessman. I believe it will hinder the development of the oil and mining industries in the west. An example of what I consider prejudice is the removal of the tax on margarine. This will certainly make some dairy products less competitive and, in the end, increase the burden on the dairy farmer. Yet, the government gives the electronics industry a boost by removing the federal excise tax. Why cannot the same consideration be given to agriculture?
I should like, Mr. Speaker, to refer for a few minutes to the implementation at this time of a capital gains tax. This is a tax at income tax rates on 50 per cent of all capital gains on property sold valued at more than $1,000. I believe this will have a very devastating and detrimental effect on the west. I can only conclude that the minister has failed to recognize the nature of the rural farm set-up on the Prairies. Is it oversight or is it a definite government policy to drive the farmer from the land? The reason the capital gains tax is unfair to the farmer is quite simple. It lies in past government farm policies. This government allowed prairie farm income to slip so badly that the only hope a farmer had was the knowledge that he owned valuable land. In the last ten years farm land has not been easy to obtain. Many young people who wished to start out in an agricultural career found that the owning of their own farm required a tremendous outlay of capital. Many such new farmers went into debt for years. They virtually signed away their futures. Profits were poured into paying for the land. The people have done without the normal amenities and luxuries of urban life in order to own their own land.
A farmer will work hard all his life in order to pay for his land. He never shows a profit until his land is paid for, perhaps some 20 or 30 years after he has begun farming. I repeat that the one thing which has kept the farmer going has been his knowledge that, on his retirement, he would own valuable land that would bring him a return for all his years of work. Now, when he sells his land he will be taxed to the hilt. This is grossly unfair. Many of these farmers have been building and paying for 30 years or more. The fruits of thirty years hard work are to be taken away. The minister should realize that farmers are not speculators. All they desire is an honest return for their years of doing without and paying for the land which they hope to own. These are not overnight gains that are being taxed in this case, but the labours of generations of work. All I can say is that I must protest this move. It will remove what little incentive there was left in the agricultural industry.
There is another aspect of the capital gains tax which is unfair, especially to rural western Canada. It is being implemented at a time when farm land values are depressed because this government has allowed the western economy to fall into a state of depression. Depending on the region, land prices have gone down 20 per cent to 30 per cent. When a farmer sells his land upon reaching retirement age, he will pay a higher than normal capital gains tax because valuation day will be at a time when the farm values are depressed. Supposedly he has a choice in determining his tax. He can use the purchase value of his farm or he can use the value as of valuation day, which is a day to be later announced. Now, if in five or six years he wishes to sell, it is quite likely that the land values will have returned to or greatly exceeded the values of five years ago. The result of all this will be a higher differential between the buying and selling price than should be the case, and because of this the farmer will be paying a disproportionate share of the capital gains tax when he disposes of his assets.
If the government insists on a capital gains tax for farmers, I hope that it will defer its implementation to a time when land values have returned to their previous level or to a more realistic level. In the case of a farmer who has owned land for 30 years and wishes to retire in five years, the tax would certainly be higher than he should be paying.
The capital gains tax cannot be called true tax reform. If anything, it is a retrogressive step. In the first place, the government has reduced the personal income tax to
61.1	per cent from 82.4 per cent for the $100,000 level. The capital gains tax, set up as it is now, will do more to establish the rich in this country as the favoured class. The capital gains tax will reduce the incentive of the middle income earners who have aspirations of becoming rich and who invest accordingly. This tax will affect the greatest source of investment capital in the country. This seems to me to be a contradiction in government policy. Two weeks ago, we were closing debate on the establishment of the Canada Development Corporation. The government rammed this bill through, saying that it. would encourage Canadian investment in Canada. Now, we have the capital gains tax which I am sure will take much of the incentive out of such investment. Perhaps the government had in mind the fact that one measure would offset the other. At the time, we expressed our doubts that the establishment of the CDC would encourage a greater degree of Canadian investment. In my opinion, the implementation of a capital gains tax will just make the situation worse, and of course if it were truly a reform it would be a progressive tax which it is not. It will hinder the middle income earner the most, and it will do much to stratify this country even more into three groups, the rich, the middle class and the poor. Upward mobility will become more difficult.
The government has been congratulating itself on this budget. They say that the tax cuts will be beneficial to the economy and that the budget will be hailed as one of tax reform. The initial reaction of the press and of

speakeroldname: Hon. John N. Turner (Minister of Justice):
speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, although I would enjoy supporting the budgetary provisions of the Minister of Finance (Mr. Benson) on behalf of the government, and indeed the substance of the changes in tax reform which he has presented for the approval of the country and of Parliament, this afternoon I want to confine my remarks to some of the procedural aspects of the income tax bill which is annexed to the resolutions, which affects taxpayers' rights as against the Crown, and which to my mind enhances the rights of the taxpayer in his dealings with the Crown.

June 28, 1971
The Budget-Hon. J. Turner
I have said on other occasions that one of the objectives of the federal Department of Justice is to attempt to redress, so far as we have jurisdiction, the imbalance of the relationship between the individual and the state, and to compensate somewhat for the remoteness, the bigness and the anonymity of government, and so to arrange the rights and remedies available to the individual citizen that he is not further obscured and dwarfed by the bigness and pervasiveness of modern government.
We undertook a review of the administrative powers available to the state contained in the present Income Tax Act. We have reviewed these powers with the purpose of seeing whether they might not be altered so as to afford the citizen greater protection from arbitrary action on the part of his government. It is important that the laws of this country should give to the citizen a clear right to air any grievance he has and, in respect of the matter now before the House, to air any grievance he has with the revenue authorities of Canada in as speedy and expeditious a manner as possible. I believe further it is essential that the rights of the individual, in so far as they relate to his duty to discharge his proper burden of taxes towards his fellow citizens, should not be unduly or unnecessarily curtailed or restricted.
Your Honour, in the annexed bill which is attached to the resolutions now before the House, there are provisions which have been inserted with the purpose of simplifying legal proceedings, of giving the Canadian taxpayer a greater right of access to the courts, of giving him the means of having legal disputes with the Crown determined in as expeditious a manner as possible, and providing him with greater protection from the arbitrary abuse of the various administrative powers now under the Income Tax Act entrusted to various officials concerned with the administration and enforcement of the revenue laws. One of the greatest protections which a citizen can have from arbitrary action is the right to institute legal proceedings for the purpose of asserting his rights. If this right or remedy is to be effective, it is necessary to see that the provisions in relation to the institution of legal proceedings be kept as simple as possible.
Hon. members will recall that when the Tax Review Board bill was before the House, it implemented the first step of the government's program to simplify legal proceedings under the Income Tax Act. That bill, which is now law, gives the average citizen a greater opportunity to challenge any assessment for tax made against him. Hon. members will recall also that under section 9 of the Tax Review Board Act, it is provided that no special type or form of pleading, or petition is required in order to institute an appeal before the board against any assessment for tax. Hon. members will also recall that the Tax Review Board, in adjudicating disputes between taxpayers and revenue authorities, is not to be bound by any legal or technical rules of evidence.
The taxpayer is not required to be represented by his lawyer. He can appear himself before the board, or be supported by his accountant, or any neighbour or friend who has some knowledge of the facts before the board.

There was also in this act, when it appeared before Parliament and as it was endorsed by Parliament, a legislative directive that the board was to deal with all appeals as informally and as expeditiously as the circumstances and considerations of fairness would permit. That act also amended the Income Tax Act to provide that if the revenue authorities were unsuccessful before the board, that is, if the taxpayer were successful in having his appeal against the assessment allowed, and the revenue authorities appealed that decision to the then Exchequer Court, now the Federal Court of Canada, if the amount in controversy were less than $2,500 the revenue authorities would be required to pay all reasonable and proper costs of the taxpayer in his appeal, whether or not the taxpayer won or lost that appeal before the court.
I think hon. members will recall that our colleague from Burnaby-Richmond-Delta was successful in persuading the standing Committee to raise that amount from $1,000 to $2,500 by way of an amended recommendation before the report stage, and we were able to endorse the comm.ttee's report. This provision with respect to the Tax Review Board has been continued in the proposed bill which is annexed to the resolutions.
In the proposed bill which is attached to the resolutions, and which is before the House, hon. members will see that further steps have now been taken to simplify legal proceedings, and to sweep away special statutory provisions found in the present Income Tax Act which in fact often constituted unnecessary and unexpected booby traps for taxpayers and for those who were advising taxpayers. In the proposals now before the House, it is provided that income tax proceedings before the Federal Court, under the Income Tax Act will be instituted in the same manner as ordinary actions. It is the view of the government that all of the various legal proceedings that may be taken under various statutes before the Federal Court of Canada should, to the greatest extent possible, correspond to those of an ordinary action in that court so that any lawyer can feel perfectly competent to institute proceedings in the Federal Court.
Hon. members will observe that the proposed bill provides that the special form on notice of appeal against an income tax assessment before the court shall no longer be necessary. In future, all proceedings will be instituted in substantially the same manner as any other legal proceeding. Furthermore, the rather incomplete and fragmentary code of procedure now found in division J of the Income Tax Act, which regulates the manner in which actions between the Crown and taxpayers are to be conducted, has been swept away. Under new provisions, the rules of the federal court will apply to legal proceedings instituted under the Income Tax Act in the court. Now, rather than having a fragmented, overly-complicated and incomplete code of procedure under which the taxpayer is governed if he wishes to challenge the assessment of the Department of National Revenue, the generalized rules of court will be available to him.
There is an adage that justice delayed is justice denied. For this reason, an attempt has been made in the pro-
June 28. 1971

posed bill to provide for alternative avenues to have disputes between the revenue authorities and the taxpayers resolved. These alternatives will permit a more expeditious resolution of disputes. For example, in many cases, at the time when the tax is assessed, it is clear to both the revenue authorities and the taxpayer that there is a serious dispute which will not be resolved on the facts of the assessment without a determination on a point of law by the courts. Hon. members will see that in the proposed bill, provision has now been made whereby a taxpayer in filing a notice of objection to the assessment can indicate that he wishes to appeal immediately to the court or tax review board. In that case, the revenue authorities, if they consent, are empowered to refer the objection immediately to the forum chosen by the taxpayer for adjudication.
Hon. members will also see that in the proposed bill there is provision that the federal court has jusrisdiction to determine any question of law, fact or mixed law and fact arising out of the bill, which the parties have, by stated case, agreed upon. This will be useful both to the taxpayer and revenue authorities. This provision will permit the question to be stated to the court prior to any assessment having been made, and thus it should be possible to obtain a decision on the question of law while the facts remain to be determined.
If hon. members have had an opportunity to go through the rather complicated provisions of the bill annexed to the resolution presented by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Benson) they will observe that the Minister of National Revenue now will be able to make an application to the federal court or to the tax revenue board to determine common questions of law, fact or mixed law and fact which are common to one or more assessments determined in a single proceeding. In other words, where there is a question of law that may affect a number of taxpayers across the country, rather than putting the burden upon a single taxpayer to go to court to have that determined, the minister may ask that a class action be taken in order that one case may be determined for the benefit of all taxpayers in a similar situation. I believe this provision will avoid multiplicity of litigation and I believe it will result in a fairer adjudication of the issues where a determination of the factual interests of one taxpayer might adversely affect another. I think every lawyer in this House has heard the saying, "hard cases make bad law". Sometimes it is the psychology of particular circumstances-

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: So do bad statutes.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
-before the court which may influence which way a decision will go. A decision which may be the proper one in terms of equity and justice for the one taxpayer may, because of law involved, prejudicially affect hundreds of thousands of other taxpayers whose rights have not been impartially determined. By allowing the case to go before the court in this way, a fairer judgment will be arrived at for all involved.
The Budget-Hon. J. Turner
Hon. members will observe specific provisions in the annexed bill allowing for appeals from the denial of registration or the revocation of registration of a charitable organization, amateur athletic association, retirement savings plan or profit sharing plan. Any hon. members who have represented sports associations seeking a certificate of deductibility for contributions under the Income Tax Act will know how difficult it is to obtain this. At the moment, there is no appeal from the decision of the administrative officers concerned. I believe an appeal from an administrative decision relating to charitable organizations, retirement savings plans and profit sharing plans is a step forward.
Any revenue law which commands the respect of the majority of citizens must contain penal provisions. There must be the mechanics available to punish that incredibly small minority of citizens not prepared to carry their fair share of the cost of providing for the common weal and the cost of government. It is equally important that those penal provisions of any Income Tax Act should not be oppressive, unfair or harsh. The procedure should be such that their application is fair and not arbitrary. For that reason, we propose to change the existing rule so that now in any case where a penalty has been assessed against a taxpayer, the burden in the event of a dispute will be on the revenue authorities to establish the facts justifying the imposition of the penalty. It is the view of this government that it is not good administration of justice to permit imposition of penalties subsequent to imposition of punishment by the courts. We do not believe it is fair administration for the Department of National Revenue to come along after a court decision adjudging guilt or liability, and add a further penalty to the result.
There is now a clear legislative intent in the present bill that no penalty can be imposed after proceedings for the commission of an offence have been instituted in the courts. It is up to the courts to decide whether the penalty can be invoked, whether interest runs and whether criminal or civil law is involved.
The wide provisions under the present section 126 (3) of the Income Tax Act permit the Minister of National Revenue to grant an authorization to enter and search the premises. This has been curtailed. Under the new provisions set forth in the annexed bill, it will be incumbent upon the revenue authorities to establish by evidence on oath to the satisfaction of a judge that there are reasonable and probable grounds for believing that a violation of the act has been committed or is likely to be committed before they are authorized to enter and search. There is no more blanket authorization to enter and search. The bill further provides that a person from whom documents have been seized will be entitled to inspect them and obtain copies. The proposed bill annexed to the resolution contains a provision which will require the revenue authorities to return any documents seized during the course of an audit to the taxpayer within 120 days from the date of seizure, unless an order is obtained from a judge of a superior or county court permitting them to be kept.

June 28, 1971
The Budget-Hon. J. Turner
Finally, the provision under which inquiries are held under the Income Tax Act has been changed substantially. First, an inquiry is now to be held before a hearing officer, a person appointed by the Tax Review Board, not an administrative officer of the department. This should give all interested parties an assurance that the hearing officer will be a person independent of the revenue authorities. The bill goes on to provide that any person giving evidence on an inquiry will be entitled to be represented by counsel and upon request will be entitled to receive a transcript of the evidence given by him before the inquiry. Provision is made for the person whose affairs are being investigated to be present and represented by counsel unless the hearing officer rules to the contrary. I believe these are all advances which are long overdue and are remedial in their purpose and intent.
I can assure hon. members and Your Honour that in arriving at these proposals put forward by the Minister of Finance on budget night, the government was assisted by representations received from interested citizens and organizations all over the country, from the committee of the Canadian Bar Association and from the institute of chartered accountants.
The administrative process remains an unexplored labyrinth. We are concerned, particularly in the Department of Justice, about the difficulty of challenging laws that may have gone beyond statutory limits or the scrutiny of Parliament. We are concerned with controlling the breadth of the enabling powers that authorize those regulations that are found in our statutes. We are concerned, as well, about the judicial powers exercised by administrative tribunals. We introduced a federal court bill, which now is law, to broaden the scope of the judicial review of the powers of administrative tribunals, commissions and boards, making them more responsive to the average Canadian citizen. This process is continuing.
The provisions I have referred to which relate to the procedural rights and remedies of the taxpayer against the state are a continuation of the civilizing of the administrative process in the service of the individual. We have to inquire into the complete workings of the public administrative law in this country, including the organization, administration and operation of the procedures of federal boards, tribunals and commissions, and into the internal workings of departments of government, to ensure that Canadians, in dealing with their government at Ottawa or across the country at the federal level, have opportunities to challenge, have remedies that are effective in the courts if that action is ineffective. We will continue to define and create new remedies and processes of review for the average Canadian citizen against the state.
I commend to the House the provisions of the proposed bill presented by the Minister of Finance that go a great distance towards redressing some of the imbalances between the citizen and his government so far as discharging his fair share of the burden of taxation is concerned.

Mr. Speaker, I will not speak on the subject which the Minister of Justice (Mr. Turner) raised. Of course, it is important; I do not deny that. I suspect that it is more important to the wealthier citizens and to the corporations than to the ordinary worker or taxpayer whose tax is deducted at source. I do not deny that the subject is important; however, that is not the subject with which I want to deal.
The more one studies the budget, the budget speech and the income tax resolution, the so-called tax reforms, the more it becomes clear that the Canadian people may be the victims of a major hoax and the more it becomes clear to me that ten years of work in seeking tax reform is now down the drain. All the studies the Carter Commission made, and the attempt to establish equity in our tax system which the Carter Commission Report presented have been entirely rejected by the government. Indeed, many of the more progressive suggestions in the white paper have been retreated from in what we now have before us.
I want to make clear on behalf of my colleagues, and the party I have the honour to lead across Canada, that we reject the notion that there has been tax reform as suggested by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Benson). There is no such thing before this House. There are some tax changes, a few of them desirable and many of them undesirable; however, the tax system which the Minister of Finance has presented and which members of the government party are supporting remains inequitable and unjust in most of its aspects. It does not reform the system; it does not shift the burden of taxation to those who can afford to pay; it does not introduce equity to our tax system. The inequities, injustices, loopholes and special privileges which have existed in the tax system until now will continue existing. Therefore, It is not a tax reform at all. I have a feeling, Mr. Speaker, that despite the attempts of the government and government spokesmen to persuade the people of Canada that the tax system of this country has really been reformed, the people of this country, the workers, farmers and the majority of our citizens and residents, will recognize very quickly that they cannot accept that proposal, that they are the victims of a hoax, that it is not true that the tax system has been made more equitable and that it will go on being just as bad as it has been until now.
There have been some desirable tax changes, Mr. Speaker. We have, at last, increases in personal exemptions, which of course everyone in Canada welcomes. I make two points about that. First, I point out, as everyone can see who has made some kind of statistical study of this, that the increases in tax exemptions are still less than would have resulted from a tabulation of the cost of living increase since 1949, when the present tax exemptions were introduced. There would need to be a considerable increase in that item. I say secondly, Mr. Speaker, that we have rejected for some time personal exemptions as an adequate or equitable way of dealing with the matter. We have insisted that there be a tax credit system, as the Carter Commission Report suggests. It is obvious to anyone who has thought about it that increases in tax exemptions benefit higher income people
June 28, 1971

a great deal more than they benefit lower income people. Having said that, I am pleased, of course, that there is to be some increase in the personal exemption. We are very pleased, indeed, that there is to be some relief for old age pensioners and aged people, and we are very pleased with the child care allowance. Those are the only improvements of substance in the new tax system that has been introduced.
What about the capital gains tax?
I will come to the capital gains tax later.
And what about the margarine tax?

I hope the hon. member will forgive me if I do not think that that is quite as important as some of the other things I have mentioned. He does not think so, either. Although I am very pleased with these things, as I said on another occasion, I did not jump for joy at these things being done. You know, Mr. Speaker, all that the Minister of Finance has done is this: He has stopped robbing the poor. He has stopped taxing those who for years should not have been on the tax rolls. While we are very pleased indeed that those poor people in Canada will no longer be gouged, even to a small extent, I cannot accept that item as being the basis for tax reform. I say that, welcome though the changes may be.
Why do I say that there is not tax reform, Mr. Speaker? I will come to the economic part of the budget later. I say that there is no tax reform for a number of reasons which I want to emphasize. All have been dealt with by the hon. member for Waterloo (Mr. Saltsman) in his excellent speech on the first day of the budget debate and by two more colleagues who followed him. I think it is important to underline these things.
First, Mr. Speaker, let me point out that much, if not most of the tax decrease for the 4 million-odd people who, according to the minister's table, are to pay decreased taxes, is due not to change in the tax system at all but to the elimination of the 3 per cent surtax. This surtax was imposed on a temporary basis and should have ended on December 31, 1970. Presumably, it would have ended on December 31, 1971 in any event, unless specifically extended by the government. As I say, much if not most of the tax relief for those 4 million-odd people results not from changes in the tax system but from the elimination of the 3 per cent surtax, which was a temporary tax in any event. Therefore, the claims being made are simply not justified in these circumstances.
It is interesting to look at the range of benefits as between lower income and higher income people, and anyone studying the figures will see, obviously, that what I am about to say is correct. I am not claiming any originality for it. The 3 per cent was a surtax on the tax payable. Obviously, those who pay higher taxes will get more relief.
It is interesting to look at the actual figures. A person with a gross income of $5,000 will get relief from the elimination of the 3 per cent surtax for the remaining six
The Budget-Mr. Lewis
months of 1971, as this comes into effect on July 1, of the magnificent sum of $1.31. A person earning $6,000 will get the magnificent relief from the elimination of the 3 per cent surtax of $3.91. A person with a gross income of $8,000 will get relief of $10.16. However, a person earning $20,000 will get relief of $73. When you get to a gross income of $50,000, there is relief of $298 in round figures. This repeats itself in every aspect of the tax system. It merely underlines the inequity which pervades and permeates our present tax system.
All the inequities and injustices remain, despite the introduction of the capital gains tax. Everyone has noticed that even though the capital gains tax has been introduced, the tax is to be at the income tax rate, but only on one half of the capital gains. Why? I don't know, except it is a deliberate intention to favour those who are able to earn their income through capital gains. There is no other reason why that is so. Some of my friends in the Progressive Conservative party are uneasy about any capital gains tax. I disagree with them on that point.
The Carter commission report was obviously right and just in emphasizing that the tax on the income of income earners ought to be based on the total income, not as to the source of their earnings. Whether a person makes that income by wage, salary or capital gains, it is still income in his pocket or, in most cases, the corporation's pocket and it ought to be taxed at the regular rate. In terms of equity and justice, there is no reason why a person who makes his income or any part of it by capital gains should pay income tax on only half whereas the ordinary salary earner, whether he makes $5,000, $15,000 or $20,000 a year, has to pay on his total taxable income. Indeed, in all cases, most of it is deducted at source. He has no opportunity to find any loophole with which to avoid any of the taxes.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Treasury Board
speechtext: Carter also recommended no tax on dividend income. Do you agree with that?

I will come to the dividend income in a moment. I say that the capital gains tax, which should have been on our tax books for years, finally introduced by this government after years of study and painful thought, still ends in an inequity. It is still an immense advantage to the rich and powerful in this country.
I ask the people of Canada and members of this House to remember this simple proposition. Every time any segment of our people get a tax advantage, the rest of the people have to pay for it in one way or another. Every time some group of citizens, whether individual or corporate, are able to pay less in taxes, the ordinary citizen has to pay more because the revenue of the government has to be raised somewhere. If it is not raised from those who have it, it has to be raised from those who do not have it. This is precisely what our tax system has done all these years and will continue to do.
As several writers have already indicated, the fact that capital gains will be taxed at the income tax rate on only one half of the capital gains will open yet another loophole for the avoidance of taxes. This morning I asked the Minister of Finance (Mr. Benson) a question with regard

June 28. 1971
The Budget-Mr. Lewis
to the tax avoidance which he mentioned in a speech. He said if he was to give all the instances of tax avoidance, it would take him a whole night or a whole week, I forget which.
This preference for capital gains will be an absolute Roman holiday for the tax lawyers and tax accountants when they look at the books of the corporations and individual rich Canadians. There will be a lot of juggling and interpretations made to place certain earnings under capital gains rather than under income. The treasury will not only lose by its failure to tax the whole of capital gams, as it should have done, but it will also lose by the immense loophole that is opened by this distinction between one kind of earning and capital gains.
My second point is that all the inequities in our system remain because the limited ceiling that was suggested in the white paper on expenses, entertainment and related matters of corporations and executives has been removed. There is now no such ceiling. All the games that have been played up until now with expense accounts, expense allowances, the expenses of corporations and their executives will continue to be played. There is nothing in the new so-called reform system that places a ceiling on expenses.
